other_moves.move: Engine competition with CFM as the baseline
other_moves.detail: We invite CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce to propose engines for the new airplane under code 7. CFM is the baseline launch engine and certifies first. A P&W or Rolls-Royce engine follows in sequence once it shows maturity and durability [BX-1298]. CFM must be able to support both our rates and our competitor's [BX-1264, BX-1325]. Goal: two or three engine sources on our narrowbody and three narrowbody engine makers in the market.

other_moves.move: Certification plan with the FAA from day one, and no production-certification concurrency
other_moves.detail: We agree a transparent certification plan with the FAA before detailed design freezes. We build no production airplanes ahead of a mature, certifiable design [BX-1263, BX-1309]. We blame no one: we own the schedule [BX-1323].

other_moves.move: No fixed-price development
other_moves.detail: Development contracts with suppliers and partners are cost-plus or risk-share, never fixed-price [BX-1262, BX-1304].

other_moves.move: Supplier readiness: keep fragile suppliers funded and hot
other_moves.detail: We fund lagging suppliers and keep them running above our rate, and we hold buffers [BX-1243, B-2330, B-2043]. Priorities: (1) engines, since LEAP-1B is the 737's sole source and engines have bound the line before [B-1449]; (2) any supplier flagged on the supplier-shortages KPI [B-2283]. The ladder: embed staff, buffer, requalify, fund, acquire. With Spirit in-house since December 2025 [BG-0064], we control the 737 fuselage.

other_moves.move: Balance sheet first in capital allocation
other_moves.detail: Debt repair stays first [BX-1305, BX-0556]. I recommend to the Board no shareholder returns and no new equity until we are solidly investment grade; the Board reserves both decisions. The $10B of undrawn revolvers stays undrawn.

other_moves.move: Stage-gated governance of the launch
other_moves.detail: Before the full Board votes, the Aerospace Safety Committee reviews the launch with the Chief Engineer's readiness view. After launch, each development stage gate is KPI-based, with no subjectivity [BX-1259]. If the plan has to move, we reset it once, conservatively, never in serial slips [BX-1318, BX-1321]. No launched programme is ever cancelled (H5).

other_moves.move: Workforce: retain, train before we build, hire in stages
other_moves.detail: One enterprise retention incentive [BX-1314]. We train before we build [BX-1258]. Engineering hiring is staged toward a peak around 2038-39, since the risk case prices talent poaching and supply-chain bottlenecks at 5 pp for 5 years from EIS.

other_moves.move: 737 MAX and 787 customer commitment
other_moves.detail: Production stability on the 737 MAX and 787 lines comes first, gated by KPIs. The new airplane is built for commonality with the 737 fleet so that our customers' transition is planned, not forced [BX-1273, BX-1274].

boeing.public_statement:
We said we'd do a new airplane when the market, the technology and Boeing were all ready. We've done the work to get here: the development programmes we had in front of us are done, and the balance sheet is back where it belongs. So today we are launching a new Boeing single-aisle airplane.

We're planning for entry into service in 2040, and that plan has headroom built into it. It is so much more important that we do this right than fast. We won't build airplanes ahead of a mature design. We'll work the certification plan with the FAA from day one. We'll develop this airplane with our suppliers on cost-plus and risk-share terms, not fixed price.

On engines, we've asked CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce to bring us their best. CFM is our baseline, and we want more than one source of supply on this airplane.

Our 737 MAX and 787 customers come first while we do this. Stable production and the KPIs decide our rates. Debt stays first in our capital allocation. I'm not going to give you any more dates today. The financials will follow our production performance. We still have a lot of work to do.
boeing.rationale:
DECISION: fps launch_10yr with fps_engine_code 7; rate_737 hold; re787 hold. This is the plan I framed (plan B), and both test memos recommend it.

1. MY RULINGS ON H1 AND H3 FOR 2030, IN WRITING, WITH EVIDENCE.
- H1 (no fps in Round 1) is LIFTED for 2030. Its 2026 grounds were the unfinished 777X and MAX 7/10 and an unrepaired balance sheet [B-2326, BX-1305], and all of them have closed:
  - the 777X was reset to first delivery in 2027 [BX-0550] and turns cash-positive from 2029 [BX-0547];
  - MAX 7/10 certification was expected in 2026 [BX-1873]. The brief reports no certification trouble, so I treat both as done (inference);
  - debt repair is complete on the GM's tracker: net debt reaches $0 at end-2029 (base) and end-2030 (stress), with no new programme;
  - in July 2026 I said we needed about two more years to be financially ready, with a launch expected around 2029-2030 [BG-0068];
  - the three work streams have converged [B-2303, BX-1296]. Market: the narrowbody demand is there, and Do Nothing loses $3.64-6.26B if Airbus moves. Boeing: finances repaired, and Pope confirms engineering can carry one clean-sheet development. Technology: GTF2 and UltraFan NB, if launched on selection, are ready in 2036 and 2037, and CFM is always ready.
  - The lift is conditional, and every condition has passed: Malave's buffer and fundability tests and Pope's readiness results.
- H3, first half (no 787 Re-engine in Round 1) no longer binds as a hard rule. Its ground was "the 777X comes first" [B-2276], and that has closed. I still HOLD the Re-engine on four grounds:
  - the Board's -$1B Downside limit: it adds -3.58 in S3 and S4;
  - my one-development-at-a-time rule [BX-1239];
  - company doctrine (profile §11.4: keep the 787 a cash source, no Re-engine before 2036);
  - the premium: holding it costs $0 in my expected column.
  H3's second half, H4, H5, H6 and H8 apply as written. H2 cannot bind (earliest EIS 2037). H7 has no trigger: the brief reports no certification trouble.

2. THE TEAM RULE.
- Malave's buffer test (slip leg = S5, the brief's Risk case; floor = Do Nothing's -3.64 less $2B = -5.64):
  - plan B passes at -0.78, $4.86B above the floor;
  - every via-Embraer row fails ($11.83-13.94B below the floor). That veto binds and I accept it.
- Pope's KPI veto does not bind: the brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. It is moot anyway, since I hold the rate.
- Everything else is my call.

3. THE GRID. Board items are the fps launch and the engine code that rides with it. rate_737 and re787 sit at their default (hold).

| Plan | S1 | S2 | S3 | S4 (expected) | S5 (risk case) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Submitted: fps 10-yr + 787 hold | +3.50 | +0.66 | +0.88 | -1.96 | -0.78 |
| Same with fps at its default (Do Nothing) | 0.00 | -3.64 | -2.62 | -6.26 | -3.64 |
| Value of the launch | +3.50 | +4.30 | +3.50 | +4.30 | +2.86 |

- The launch beats Do Nothing by more than ε in every column, so debt-first passes. The grid already nets the discounted debt penalty; I do not subtract it again. Undiscounted, for scale only: 10-year $19.1B, 7-year $22.0B, via Embraer $52.5B.
- Worst column: -1.96 (S4). In no column does the item lose more than $1B against its default.

4. RAMP: 10-YEAR OVER 7-YEAR.
- Against the 7-year the 10-year is +1.30 / -0.46 / +1.30 / -0.46 / +0.05. It is ahead in three columns, more than ε ahead in two, and behind only by 0.46 in S2 and S4, inside ε. Its mean across the five columns is +0.46 against the 7-year's +0.11.
- In my expected S4 the 7-year is the best grid plan by $0.46B. That is a tie, and the team rule breaks it on doing less, better [BX-1239] and the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548]. Both point to the 10-year:
  - a $4.68B smaller bill and $2.9B less undiscounted debt penalty;
  - a 2036 cash peak of about $8.4B against about $12.5B in 2034;
  - every debt line kept, the stress case included (peak $0.0B). The 7-year borrows $0.7B under stress and is still above zero at the 2035 hold year;
  - three years of headroom against our clean-sheet slip record (787-8: May 2008 to September 2011 [B-0031, B-0526]), and no production-certification concurrency [BX-1263], which is my red line.
- The 7-year's S2/S4 edge and its incumbency in 2040 both exist only if it meets NGSA's 2037 EIS to the year. A three-year slip turns it into the 10-year airplane with a bigger bill. Airbus's timeline does not set our date [B-2313].
- Doctrine also points to the 10-year ramp: profile §11.4, "Ramp-up speed: the 10-year ramp".

5. OBJECTIVE LEDGER (Control's mission; it never changes the payoff).
- Debt: plan B reads 2029 / yes / yes ($0.0B) in every column. The 7-year misses the stress line in every column.
- Incumbency, by my sketch of the public share rules:
  - the 10-year holds 40% or more throughout in S1 and S3, but dips to about 37% in 2040 in S2 and S4 (about 32% in S5). It recovers to about 42% by 2045 and about 47% by 2050 on the 3-year lead rule;
  - the 7-year holds in S1-S4 and dips to about 38% in 2040 in S5.
- In every column the 10-year misses no more objectives than the 7-year: S2/S4 trade one miss for one, and in S1, S3 and S5 the 7-year misses more.
- 50/50 is out of reach for every plan.
- I weigh debt, which is on my own ranked list [BX-1305], above an incumbency gain that depends on a schedule our record says we would not hold.

6. 787 RE-ENGINE: hold.
- It adds +2.20 in S1, S2 and S5 and -3.58 in S3 and S4. That is a bet on an A350 choice we cannot see, and it fails the Board's -$1B Downside limit.
- In S4 holding it costs nothing.
- The cost I accept, unpriced: on the 10-year a 2035 Re-engine would overlap 5 years and break H4, so the next H4-legal round is 2045. Widebody growth comes from Charleston capacity [BX-1317], and the 787 stays a cash source. Doctrine, not my record, drives this.

7. RATE INCREASE: hold.
- It adds -0.74 in every column beside the launch, so it fails its business case. Its +2.30 alone needs fps on hold and S1 or S3, and even then it assumes neither new narrowbody is ever launched.
- This is the only round the board offers it, so the deferral is a loss I accept, not a wait.
- It is not a reply to anyone (H6).

8. ENGINE CODE 7: costs nothing on the board.
- On today's record the fitted source at a 2040 EIS is CFM (1).
- If P&W (GTF2, ready 2036) and Rolls-Royce (UltraFan NB, ready 2037) launch on selection this round, both are ready 4 and 3 years before EIS: three sources by 2050 and three narrowbody engine makers.
- Code 7 is in no disallowed pair. Doctrine and my Low-confidence lean were code 3; code 7 keeps CFM as the fallback and serves the supply-stability enabler.

9. PREMIUM (H8): $0.46B, logged.
- What it is: the 10-year against the best S4 plan (7-year), counted in S2 and S4.
- Why: doctrine (higher-confidence plan with headroom, doing less, no concurrency) plus objective (the stress-case debt line).
- Re-engine hold $0, rate hold $0, code $0. Total $0.46B, $1.54B inside the cap.
- What would break it: an expected column of S1, S2 or S5, where the Re-engine hold would read $2.20B. In that case the hold rests on the Board's veto and H-rules, not on doctrine.

10. DEBT PATH, plan B (Malave's reconstruction, matching the brief's cells within $0.05B):
- base net debt $16.5B (2027), $6.7B (2028), $0 every year from 2029;
- stress $18.3B, $11.7B, $3.3B, then $0 from 2030, with at least $2.5B of headroom (2036);
- programme cash: about $3.0B in 2030, rising to about $8.4B in 2036;
- no new equity and no shareholder return in the plan.

memo_weighing.cfo:
Both seats are thin, and I weighed them that way. Malave's record is one call (Low), so I treated his buffer test as binding and the rest of his memo as advice.

Binding: every Solo row passes the slip leg, and plan B sits $4.86B above the -5.64 floor. Every via-Embraer row fails, and I accept that veto.

Advice I adopted:
- Fundable when the 777X turns: a pass. The 777X is cash-positive from 2029 [BX-0547], and both ramps meet the end-2030 deadline.
- His balance-sheet tie-break between the ramps: a $4.68B smaller bill, $2.9B less undiscounted penalty, and the stress debt line kept.
- His cash paths for plans B and C, which put the 7-year's $0.7B stress peak at end-2034, still above zero at the 2035 hold year.
- His $0.46B premium figure and its cap check.
- His advice to hold the Re-engine and the rate.

Two points I noted and did not act on. The 7-year's gap might close if the Board retained the 2030-33 surplus, but the GM scores the tracker as written. And the 2035 Re-engine option that only the 7-year keeps open is unpriced on this grid. I name both in the rationale.

recommendations.text: Rule on H1 and H3 in writing. Both were written for a round sealed in 2026, and this round is 2030. The record we expect cited: the 777X was reset to first delivery in 2027, MAX 7/10 certification was expected in 2026, and the 777X was due to turn cash-positive in 2029. The CEO said in July 2026 that Boeing needed about two more years to be financially ready. The brief's tracker has net debt at $0 by 2029, and at $0 in the 2030 stress case. If the conditions are met, say so and lift H1. Without that ruling, a launch fails our Boeing-ready test.

Bring one well-founded Solo fps launch, not a bet. Either ramp passes all our tests. They differ by more than ε in S1 and S3 (10-year ahead by $1.30B), so our rule prefers the ramp with the higher worst column: the 7-year (-1.50 against -1.96 in S4). It also enters service in 2037, the same year as an NGSA launched now. By our reading of the public rules, Boeing then stays at or above 40% of the narrowbody market. The 10-year would leave Boeing near 37% around 2040 if Airbus launches now. If the ExCo prefers the 10-year to keep the stress-case debt line (the 7-year peaks at $0.7B of net debt), we will approve it. Log the $0.46B it gives up in S2 and S4 as objective premium.

No 787 Re-engine this round. It loses $2.48B to $4.51B whenever Airbus re-engines the A350 (S3, S4), beyond our $1B limit. With the 7-year fps it also overlaps development by 5 years. Test it again in the 2035 round, when Airbus's A350 choice is public. A 7-year fps (development 2030-2037) leaves room for a Re-engine launched in 2035 with only a 2-year overlap. A 10-year fps (development 2033-2040) does not.

Treat the Rate Increase as a production call on its own merits. With any fps launch it loses $0.74B in every column; it pays only if neither new narrowbody is ever launched. Bring it only with fps: hold, stable KPIs, an FAA-cleared rate path and a reason that is not Airbus.

Choose fps_engine_code 7 (Rolls-Royce, P&W and CFM). CFM is always fitted, so supply is never left without an engine. The code can trigger P&W's and Rolls-Royce's conditional launches this round. GTF2 would be ready in 2036 and UltraFan NB in 2037, both by either EIS. That gives the brief's three sources on the fps in 2050, and three narrowbody engine makers, against one with Do Nothing. Code 7 is in none of the disallowed pairs, and the code does not change Boeing's payoff. We will ask our Aerospace Safety Committee to review each maker's readiness for EIS.

Show the debt path for the chosen plan, base and stress case, from the brief's objective-metrics table. Keep shareholder returns off and seek no new equity until the rating is solidly investment grade. The Board reserves those decisions.

In the public statement, give a conservative EIS with headroom if fps launches, and no date otherwise. Log every premium. Bring the launch to the Aerospace Safety Committee with the Chief Engineer's readiness view before the full Board votes.

frame.question: Have the three work streams converged by 2030: the market, Boeing's readiness in finances and capacity, and the technology? If they have, I lift H1 and launch one Solo fps. That leaves three questions: which ramp (7-year or 10-year); whether the 787 Re-engine and the 737 Rate Increase stay out of this round; and which engine code gives us a stable supply of engines from more than one maker. The grid, Malave's slip leg (S5) and Pope's readiness results decide this. Airbus's calendar does not.
frame.situation:
Decision year 2030. Nothing is launched; we are on the 737 MAX and the 787. Do Nothing scores +0.00 / -3.64 / -2.62 / -6.26 / -3.64. The columns are S1 rivals hold, S2 NGSA, S3 A350 Re-engine, S4 both, and S5 the risk case (NGSA plus covert Delay Tactics).

The brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem and no certification trouble, so the KPI gate and the FAA-process gate are open on this board.

The gates behind H1 and H3:
- 777X first delivery in 2027 [BX-0550], cash-positive from 2029 [BX-0547];
- MAX 7/10 certification expected in 2026 [BX-1873]. The brief is silent on it, so I treat it as done (inference);
- the GM's tracker puts net debt at $0 at end-2029 in the base case and at end-2030 in the stress case, with no new programme;
- in July 2026 I said we needed about two more years to be financially ready, and reporting expected a launch around 2029-2030 [BG-0068].

What the grid shows:
- Either Solo fps beats Do Nothing by more than ε in every column: 10-year +3.50 / +4.30 / +3.50 / +4.30 / +2.86; 7-year +2.20 / +4.76 / +2.20 / +4.76 / +2.81.
- The 10-year leads the 7-year by 1.30 in S1 and S3, trails it by 0.46 in S2 and S4, and is 0.05 ahead in S5. It is never behind by more than ε.
- Via Embraer runs $18.05-18.06B below the 10-year in every column.
- The 787 Re-engine adds +2.20 to the 10-year in S1, S2 and S5 but -3.58 in S3 and S4. On the 7-year it adds +1.27 or -4.51, with a 5-year overlap.
- The Rate Increase costs 0.74 in every column beside any fps. Alone it is +2.30 only in S1 and S3, and only if neither new narrowbody is ever launched.

Objective status:
- 50% narrowbody share in 2040 is out of reach for every plan.
- The 10-year keeps every debt line, the stress case included (peak $0.0B). By my reading of the public rules it leaves us near 37% in 2040 if NGSA launches now.
- The 7-year holds 40% or more against NGSA but misses the stress-case debt line (peak $0.7B).
- In S5 both ramps dip below 40% around 2040.
- Engine table: every code gives CFM only until P&W or Rolls-Royce launch. Code 7 can trigger both: 3 sources in 2050.

Board risks (its would-veto list; guidance, not red lines):
- fps via Embraer;
- any re787 launch this round;
- a Rate Increase beside any fps, or one that loses value, meets a live problem or answers Airbus;
- any fps without my H1 ruling, Malave's buffer and fundability results and Pope's readiness results;
- any premium above $2B, or any premium not logged.

red_lines: H1 (no fps in Round 1). My ruling: lifted for 2030. Its 2026 grounds have closed: the 777X delivers from 2027 [BX-0550] and is cash-positive from 2029 [BX-0547]; MAX 7/10 certification was expected in 2026 [BX-1873]; net debt is at $0 in 2029 (base) and 2030 (stress) on the GM's tracker; in July 2026 I said about two more years [BG-0068]; and the three work streams have converged [BX-1296, B-2303, B-2326]. The lift is conditional: if Malave's buffer or fundability test fails, or Pope's readiness check fails, H1 stands and we hold.

H3, first half (no 787 Re-engine in Round 1). My ruling: its ground was that the 777X comes first [B-2276], and that ground has closed, so it no longer binds as a hard rule in 2030. The Re-engine is still governed by H3's second half, by H4 and by my one-development-at-a-time rule [BX-1239].
H2 cannot bind (the earliest fps EIS is 2037). H7 has no trigger on this board.

H5: never cancel a launched fps or 787 Re-engine. Re-baseline once instead [BX-1251, BX-1321].
H6: no Rate Increase under a live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem, and never as a reply to Airbus [BX-1259, BX-1322].
H8: ties within ε ($1B) go to doctrine. Doctrine plus objective premium may total at most $2B, and every premium is logged.

My own: no production-certification concurrency [BX-1263]; no new airplane before debt repair and finished developments, which I rule met in 2030 [BX-1247, B-2326]; no fixed-price development, only cost-plus or risk-share terms [BX-1262, BX-1304]; no blame on the FAA [BX-1323]; no attribution of a supplier problem to Airbus before exposure (doctrine).
frame.asks_ops:
Stephanie, your seat runs on the operations doctrine. I need results more than views: the Board will not vote a launch without them.

1. **KPIs.** The brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. Confirm that your KPI veto does not bind. Is the 737 line stable at its current rate on an FAA-agreed path? (47 a month was cleared in May 2026; 52 depends on the new Everett line [BG-0069].) This matters only if a Rate Increase stays on the table.
2. **Two-front strain.** The fps alone carries none. The 10-year plus a 2030 Re-engine overlaps in 2033-35: 2 years, $1.2B undiscounted. The 7-year plus a Re-engine overlaps 5 years and is struck under H4. Can engineering carry one clean-sheet development alongside the 737, 787 and 777X lines?
3. **Ramp.** Can a 7-year development be done without production-certification concurrency [BX-1263] under today's certification process [BX-1309]? Or does only the 10-year leave the headroom I plan with [BX-1275]?
4. **Suppliers.** With Spirit now in-house [BG-0064], is the supply base ready to take a new airplane on cost-plus or risk-share terms while holding today's rates? Which fragile suppliers must we fund to keep hot?
5. **Engines on code 7** (Rolls-Royce, P&W and CFM):
   - What do up to three engine options add to integration, certification and durability risk [BX-1298], against codes 6, 5 or 3?
   - CFM is always fitted. GTF2 would be ready in 2036 and UltraFan NB in 2037 if they launch this round.
   - Does a 2040 EIS count as "in production" for the 2040 engine-source year?
6. **Solo or via Embraer, on IP** [BX-1330]. Does Embraer bring anything we lack that is worth a $100B bill and $52.5B of debt penalty?
7. **Workforce.** What is our exposure to talent poaching in the risk case, and how do we absorb it?
frame.initial_lean:
My lean: launch one Solo fps on the 10-year ramp with fps_engine_code 7. rate_737 hold. re787 hold. Expected column: Airbus launches NGSA this round. I take S4 under the doctrine fallback (profile §7 expects an early A350 Re-engine attempt), with S2 close behind; S5 is the risk case.

1. **Launch.** I lift H1 on the evidence above. Market, money and technology converge in 2030, and the grid agrees: the 10-year beats Do Nothing by $2.86-4.30B in every column, well past ε, and sits $4.86B above Malave's floor. "We will do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready" [BX-1296]. I think we are.

2. **Ramp.** In S4 the 7-year is the best grid plan by 0.46. That is within ε, so it is a tie, and doctrine breaks it:
   - doing less, better, with headroom, and right rather than fast [BX-1239, BX-1241, BX-1275];
   - a smaller bill and a smaller debt penalty;
   - every debt line kept, the stress case included.
   The 7-year's edge in S2 and S4 comes only from matching NGSA's 2037 EIS, and Airbus does not set our date [B-2313].
   Premium: 0.46 in S2 and S4, logged as doctrine plus objective (the debt line), well inside the $2B cap. The cost on the mission side is incumbency near 37% in 2040 if NGSA launches now. I will weigh that against the 7-year's $0.7B stress-case miss once I have both memos.

3. **No 787 Re-engine.** It wins 2.20 or loses 3.58 on an A350 choice we cannot see. In S4 it is a loss, so holding it costs no premium. One development at a time.

4. **No Rate Increase.** It loses 0.74 in every column beside a launch. I accept the loss of the only round it is offered.

5. **Code 7.** It keeps CFM fitted, invites P&W and Rolls-Royce, and costs nothing on the board. It aims at three engine sources and three narrowbody engine makers.

**Other moves.** Private: fund supplier readiness. Public: say we welcome proposals from all three engine makers, with CFM as the baseline.

**Public statement.** Calm, about execution. A conservative EIS with headroom, and no blame for anyone.

**What would change my lean:** a failed buffer or fundability test, a readiness gap in Pope's results, or evidence that only the 7-year keeps us whole.

Cash is not the objection (tracker stress peak $0.0B); the downside is.

vetoes.plan: rate_737: increase (with any fps, or alone with S4 expected)
vetoes.ground: Advice only: -0.74 or -0.75 in every column beside any fps, and -0.74 alone in the expected S4. It fails its business case. The rate gate itself is Pope's call (KPI, FAA-agreed path); H6 forbids it as a reply to Airbus.

vetoes.plan: fps: launch_7yr in place of launch_10yr
vetoes.ground: Advice only: it passes my buffer test (S5 -0.83), so I have no veto. On the balance sheet it is the weaker plan: it misses the stress-case debt line (peak $0.7B at end-2034, still above zero at the 2035 hold year), carries a $4.68B larger bill and $2.9B more undiscounted penalty, and peaks near $12.5B of cash in one year against $8.4B. Its 0.46 edge in S2 and S4 is inside epsilon.

cfo.would_change_mind_if: Five things would change my mind. (1) A brief or tracker showing the 10-year missing a debt line, or the 7-year keeping the stress line, for example if the GM scored the 2030-33 surplus as retained, which is how the Board actually runs capital allocation. (2) Pope reporting that a 7-year development needs no production-certification concurrency and carries real schedule margin, while the ExCo weights incumbency in 2040 (the 10-year leaves us near 37% against an NGSA launched now) above the stress-case debt line. Even then the 7-year's 0.46 S4 edge stays inside epsilon. (3) The ExCo's expected column moving to S1, S2 or S5: holding the Re-engine would then read a $2.20B premium, over the cap. (4) Any live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem: that reopens H6 and H7. (5) A risk-case result for the chosen plan falling by more than $4.86B, which would take it below the -5.64 floor. I would also revisit the 10-year if the ExCo valued keeping a 2035 Re-engine H4-legal, which only the 7-year allows; that option is not priced on this grid.
cfo.memo:
Kelly, I ran the slip leg as the baseline, not a sensitivity. Do Nothing's risk case is -3.64, so the floor is -5.64. Every Solo row clears it: the 10-year at -0.78, the 7-year at -0.83, the 10-year with the Re-engine at +1.42, the rate rows at -1.52 and -1.57. Every via-Embraer row fails, $11.83-13.94B below the floor. That veto binds.

The 777X turned cash-positive in 2029 and net debt reaches zero in 2029, 2030 under stress. A 2030 launch is fundable.

The 10-year is the higher-confidence plan from a schedule and cost perspective: the 7-year with three years of buffer built in, for a $4.68B smaller bill and $2.9B less undiscounted penalty. Its peak cash year, about $8.4B in 2036, leaves roughly $2.5B of headroom with free cash flow one-third below consensus, and it keeps every debt line. The 7-year peaks near $12.5B in 2034, borrows $0.7B under stress and is still above zero at the 2035 hold year. Its 0.46 lead in S4 sits inside epsilon; I log that $0.46B as premium, well inside the $2B cap.

Hold the Re-engine: it clears my buffer but loses 3.58 if Airbus re-engines the A350. Hold the rate: it loses 0.74 in every column beside a launch.

This baseline lets us not only meet it but potentially beat it, barring free cash flow more than half below consensus in the peak years. Fully restoring the health of our balance sheet stays first.

tests.name: On-time, predictable delivery [record BX-1331, applied to airplanes by inference; slip prior is doctrine/inference, profile.md §3]
tests.threshold: Can the plan's EIS be delivered as stated? Read the risk-case column (S5: NGSA plus covert Delay Tactics) and say how much of the plan's value depends on the nominal date.
tests.numbers: 10-year (EIS 2040): S2 +0.66 to S5 -0.78, so Delay Tactics cost $1.44B; it keeps +2.86 of its +4.30 gain over Do Nothing (66.5%). 7-year (EIS 2037): S2 +1.12 to S5 -0.83, cost $1.95B; it keeps +2.81 of +4.76 (59%). The board prices no schedule slip, so I read our own record. Clean-sheet prior: +3 years central, range +2 to +5 (profile §3, inference). The 787-8 was planned for May 2008 and delivered in September 2011 [B-0031, B-0526]. Certification has paced every programme since 2019 [B-2343]. The 10-year's 2040 date is the 7-year's central slip case. The 7-year's 0.46 edge in S2 and S4 exists only if it meets NGSA's 2037 EIS to the year (same-EIS rule). Under the lead rule, each year of slip gives Airbus 1 pp of share for good. A 3-year slip turns it into the 10-year airplane with a $4.68B larger bill: about $1.16B of PV at 10.5%, before the debt penalty (my arithmetic). Pass for the 10-year; the 7-year depends on its nominal date.

tests.name: Ramp choice: 10-year, EIS 2040 [inference on BX-1331; doctrine BX-1263, BX-1275, B-0373] (CEO ask 3)
tests.threshold: Operations can deliver the ramp on time with the workforce, suppliers and engines in the brief, without production-certification concurrency, and with headroom
tests.numbers: Bill $60.32B. Strain $0 alone; $1.2B with a 2030 Re-engine (overlap 2033-35, 2 years). On the 10-year, new-airplane R&D starts 5-6 years before first delivery [B-0373], about 2034-35. That is well after the 777X (first delivery 2027) and MAX 7/10 (certification expected 2026, which I infer is done). Headroom of 3 years against our clean-sheet slip prior [BX-1275]. If launched this round, GTF2 (ready 2036) and UltraFan NB (ready 2037) get 4 and 3 years of maturity before EIS. There is time to certify without building ahead of the design [BX-1263]. Cost to the Re-engine option: against this ramp, a Re-engine launched in 2035 would overlap 5 years (2035-40) and fail H4. The next H4-legal round is 2045.

tests.name: Ramp choice: 7-year, EIS 2037 [inference on BX-1331; doctrine BX-1263, BX-1309, B-2343] (CEO ask 3)
tests.threshold: Same test: on-time delivery with headroom and no production-certification concurrency under today's certification process
tests.numbers: Bill $65.00B. Strain $0 alone, but $3.0B and a 5-year overlap with a 2030 Re-engine (fails H4). The ramp has zero headroom against a slip prior of +2 to +5 years. A new airplane needs a refined FAA process [BX-1309], and certification has been the pacing item [B-2343]. Holding 2037 invites building while certifying, which our record calls 'a disaster' [BX-1263]. Engine maturity before EIS: GTF2 1 year, UltraFan NB 0 years (ready 2037 = EIS). In its favour: it keeps a 2035 Re-engine H4-legal (overlap 2035-37, 2 years), and the fps is surely in production by 2040 for the engine-source year. This is advice, not a veto: the grid has the 10-year 0.46 behind in S2/S4 (within ε) and 1.30 ahead in S1/S3.

tests.name: Two-front strain and engineering capacity [doctrine B-0341, H4; arithmetic from dashboard_game.md §2] (CEO ask 2)
tests.threshold: A Solo fps and the 787 Re-engine overlap by at most 2 years. Strain is $3B × overlap ÷ 5 (fps EIS-7 to EIS; Re-engine EIS-5 to EIS). One major development at a time
tests.numbers: Recommended plan (10-year, re787 hold): overlap 0, strain $0. 10-year plus a 2030 Re-engine: 2033-35, 2 years, $1.2B undiscounted, H4-legal. The Re-engine adds +2.20/+2.20/-3.58/-3.58/+2.20. 7-year plus Re-engine: 2030-35, 5 years, $3.0B; it fails H4 and adds +1.27/+1.27/-4.51/-4.51/+1.28. Engineering can carry one clean-sheet development alongside the 737, 787 and 777X production lines. Those are production, not development: by 2030 the 777X has been delivering since 2027 and MAX 7/10 certification is behind us (brief silent; inference). The fps would be the one major development [B-0341].

tests.name: Invest or partner on IP: Solo vs via Embraer [record BX-1330, BX-1333; applied by inference] (CEO ask 6)
tests.threshold: Solo where Boeing owns the airframe IP; via Embraer only if the partner adds what Boeing lacks (capital, capacity, time)
tests.numbers: Pass for Solo; via Embraer fails. Via Embraer has the same EIS as the 10-year (2040) and the same share rule, and gives no strain relief on the board: only the cost differs. Bill $100B vs $60.32B (+$39.68B); debt penalty $52.5B vs $19.1B undiscounted (+$33.4B). Grid -14.55/-17.39/-17.18/-20.01/-18.83, which is $18.05-18.06B below the 10-year Solo in every column. S5 is $13.19B below Malave's -5.64 floor. Stress-case peak net debt $3.3-3.7B (misses the line). Embraer brings nothing we lack worth the bill, and the airframe IP is ours to leverage.

tests.name: KPI gate for the Rate Increase: my veto [doctrine B-2221, B-2351, B-2308; not my record] (CEO ask 1)
tests.threshold: No Rate Increase while a quality, FAA or supply-chain problem is live. Steps of 5 a month, at least 6 months apart. Supplier readiness is a hard gate
tests.numbers: The gate is open and my veto does not bind: the brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. Last evidence on the line: 42 a month cleared October 2025, 47 cleared at an FAA capstone review in May 2026; 52 depends on the new Everett line [BG-0069]. The brief is silent on 2030 KPIs, so I read the line as stable at its FAA-agreed rate (inference). Scale: +5 pp of 2,000 is +100 aircraft a year, about +8.3 a month. That is more than one step of 5, so it needs at least two FAA-reviewed steps 6 or more months apart before 2032. It would take us into the zone beyond 47 where the supply chain binds [B-2340], so supplier readiness would be the gate if the Rate Increase were ordered. I do not recommend it.

tests.name: Capacity follows demand: Rate Increase rows [inference on BX-1329]
tests.threshold: Demand is fixed at 2,000 narrowbodies a year. Back the Rate Increase only where it adds value against the same plan without it in the expected column; otherwise not applicable
tests.numbers: I do not back it. Beside the 10-year it adds -0.74 in every column. Beside the 7-year: -0.74/-0.74/-0.75/-0.75/-0.74. Alone (fps hold) it adds +2.30 in S1 and S3 only, and only if neither new narrowbody is ever launched; -0.74 in S2, S4 and S5. In Ortberg's expected column (S4, with S2 close) it adds -0.74. There is no visible demand to add capacity for. Bill $2.94B, about $1.0B a year 2030-32.

tests.name: Working capital and cash conversion [record BX-1327, BX-1332, BX-1326; applied by inference]
tests.threshold: For each option: when the bill lands and what it does to cash, as a number. The stress-case debt line must hold
tests.numbers: Pass for the 10-year. 10-year: $60.32B over 2030-40 on the brief's curve: year 1 at 5% = $3.0B, average $6.0B a year, peak at 14% about $8.4B in 2036. At the tracker's 79% factor the peak is about $6.7B, against $13.8B base and $9.2B stress free cash flow. Net debt stays $0.0B in base and stress (stress peak $0.0B). 7-year: $65.00B over 2030-37, average $9.3B a year (about $7.3B at 79%, 80% of stress free cash flow before peak loading); stress peak $0.7B, which misses the line. Re-engine: $5B over 2030-35 (about $1.0B a year), plus $1.2B of strain beside the 10-year. Via Embraer: about $10B a year; stress peak $3.3-3.7B. Sensitivity: each $1B of bill booked at 2040 costs about $0.25B of PV, and about $0.33B at 2037 (10.5% WACC; the debt penalty comes on top).

tests.name: Supplier readiness for the fps while holding today's rates [doctrine B-2308, B-2330, B-2043, BX-1243] (CEO ask 4)
tests.threshold: The supply base can take a new airplane on cost-plus or risk-share terms without destabilising the 737/787/777X lines; fragile suppliers identified and funded
tests.numbers: This passes with a condition. With Spirit in-house since December 2025 [BG-0064], the 737 fuselage is ours to control. The brief reports no supply-chain problem. On the 10-year, fps supplier ramp loads land in the late 2030s, after any rate step and well after 2032. The condition is a private 'other move' that the board does not price: keep fragile or lagging suppliers hot and above our rate [BX-1243, B-2330] and hold buffers [B-2043]. Two supplier groups to fund and keep hot: (1) engines, since CFM LEAP-1B is the 737's sole source and engines have bound the line before [B-1449]; (2) any supplier flagged on the 'supplier shortages' KPI [B-2283]. Ladder: embed staff, buffer, requalify, fund, acquire (profile §3). No fixed-price development terms.

tests.name: Engine integration, certification and durability on code 7 [inference; doctrine BX-1298] (CEO ask 5)
tests.threshold: The code gives more than one source without adding unmanaged integration, certification or durability risk at EIS
tests.numbers: Pass on the 10-year. Code 7 means up to three engine-airframe integration and certification campaigns, against two for codes 5 and 6 and one for code 3. Code 3 adds none but leaves us single-source, as the 737 MAX is today (CFM, 1). CFM is always fitted. If P&W and Rolls-Royce launch on selection, GTF2 (2036) and UltraFan NB (2037) are ready 4 and 3 years before a 2040 EIS (1 and 0 years before 2037). That leaves time to certify CFM as the launch engine and sequence the other two behind it, and gives durability margin [BX-1298]. Sources in 2050: 1, or 3 if both launch. Code 7 is in no disallowed pair, and the board puts no cost on it. On 'in production in 2040': an airplane delivering from its EIS year is in production operationally, but the brief's objective table reports only 2050, so I treat the 2040 count as at risk on the 10-year. The GM's scoring decides.

tests.name: Trained workforce: talent-poaching exposure in the risk case [inference; doctrine BX-1314, BX-1258, B-0373] (CEO ask 7)
tests.threshold: The plan absorbs Delay Tactics (talent poaching and/or supply-chain bottleneck) and still beats Do Nothing and Malave's -5.64 floor
tests.numbers: On the board, one or both Delay Tactics cost the same: 5 pp for 5 years from fps EIS. Exposure: $1.44B on the 10-year and $1.95B on the 7-year (S2 to S5). Both still beat Do Nothing in S5 (+2.86, +2.81) and sit $4.86B and $4.81B above the -5.64 floor. How we absorb it (not priced on the board): one enterprise incentive for retention [BX-1314]; train before we build [BX-1258]; staged hiring, since on the 10-year the engineering peak comes 1-2 years before first delivery, about 2038-39 [B-0373]; buffers and hot suppliers against a bottleneck.

vetoes.plan: rate_737: increase (with any fps value)
vetoes.ground: My KPI veto does NOT bind this round: the brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem (team rule, teams.md §9, applies only under a live problem). Advice only: it adds -0.74/-0.75 in every column beside any fps, and -0.74 in the expected column even alone. Its +5 pp (about +8 a month) needs two or more FAA-reviewed steps into the zone beyond 47 where the supply chain binds, so supplier readiness would gate it. Under H6 it may never be a reply to Airbus.

vetoes.plan: fps: launch_7yr + re787: launch
vetoes.ground: H4 hard-rule flag, not my veto: development overlap 2030-35 is 5 years, above the 2-year cap; strain $3.0B undiscounted. Grid +3.47/+2.39/-4.93/-6.01/+0.45; stress-case peak net debt $2.8-3.1B. The rule binds the CEO.

vetoes.plan: fps: launch_10yr + re787: launch
vetoes.ground: Advice, not binding. It is H4-legal (2033-35, 2 years, $1.2B strain), but it is a second major development at once, against the one-at-a-time doctrine. The Re-engine adds +2.20 in S1, S2 and S5 and -3.58 in S3 and S4, a bet on an A350 choice we cannot see.

vetoes.plan: fps: launch_via_embraer (any row)
vetoes.ground: Advice, not binding: it fails my invest-or-partner test. Same EIS 2040 and no strain relief; +$39.68B of bill and +$33.4B of undiscounted debt penalty; $18.05-18.06B below the 10-year Solo in every column; S5 is $13.19B below the -5.64 floor.

vetoes.plan: fps: launch_7yr (Solo)
vetoes.ground: Advice, not binding. It has no schedule headroom against our clean-sheet slip prior (+2 to +5 years), and UltraFan NB would be ready only in the EIS year itself. Its 0.46 edge in S2/S4 depends on meeting 2037 to the year. If the CEO and the Board choose it, my condition is that we hold a no-concurrency rule and sequence the certification of each engine, with CFM first.

ops.would_change_mind_if: Five things would change my mind. (1) If the brief reported a live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem, my KPI veto would bind on any Rate Increase. A live certification problem would also fail the FAA-reform gate [BX-1309], and I would recommend holding the fps. (2) I would accept the 7-year on evidence that it can hold 2037 without concurrency: a refined FAA certification process, supplier and engine-maker commitments, and GTF2 and UltraFan NB ready with about 3 years of margin before 2037. I would also accept it if Malave's slip leg showed that only the 7-year passes. (3) I would back a partner if it brought capital (a share of the bill) or capacity (strain relief) that Boeing lacks. On this board Embraer brings neither. (4) For the Re-engine, Airbus's A350 choice would need to be public with no A350 Re-engine. But beside a 10-year fps the next H4-legal round is 2045, and Ortberg should weigh that now. (5) I would back a Rate Increase only with fps on hold, an expected column of S1 or S3, stable KPIs and supplier readiness beyond 47.
ops.memo:
Three results, ranked. My record is Global Services, not Commercial Airplanes, so the KPI, strain and supplier results run on Boeing's operations doctrine, and I say so.

First and foremost, on-time predictable delivery. I can stand behind 2040. Our clean-sheet record runs about three years late: the 787-8 went from May 2008 to September 2011. The 10-year date is the 7-year's central slip case, so it carries that headroom without building while we certify. It also gives GTF2 four years and UltraFan NB three years of maturity before entry into service; on the 7-year, UltraFan is ready in the EIS year itself.

Second, readiness. The brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem, so my KPI veto does not bind. The fps alone carries zero strain and is our one major development. We fund fragile suppliers and keep them hot.

Third, IP. The airframe is ours: Solo. Embraer adds nothing we lack, only $39.68B more bill and $18.05-18.06B less value in every column.

And finally, disciplined profitable growth. Every $1B booked at 2040 costs about $0.25B of PV. The 10-year's peak year draws about $8.4B, about $6.7B after the tracker's 79% factor, against $13.8B of free cash flow, and the stress-case debt line holds at $0.0B. The Rate Increase loses $0.74B in every column beside the fps: hold. The 787 Re-engine is a bet on Airbus's A350 choice: hold.

My orders: fps launch_10yr, engine code 7, rate_737 hold, re787 hold.

other_moves.move: Engine competition with CFM as the baseline
other_moves.detail: We invite CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce to propose engines for the new airplane under code 7. CFM is the baseline launch engine and certifies first. A P&W or Rolls-Royce engine follows in sequence once it shows maturity and durability [BX-1298]. CFM must be able to support both our rates and our competitor's [BX-1264, BX-1325]. Goal: two or three engine sources on our narrowbody and three narrowbody engine makers in the market.

other_moves.move: Certification plan with the FAA from day one, and no production-certification concurrency
other_moves.detail: We agree a transparent certification plan with the FAA before detailed design freezes. We build no production airplanes ahead of a mature, certifiable design [BX-1263, BX-1309]. We blame no one: we own the schedule [BX-1323].

other_moves.move: No fixed-price development
other_moves.detail: Development contracts with suppliers and partners are cost-plus or risk-share, never fixed-price [BX-1262, BX-1304].

other_moves.move: Supplier readiness: keep fragile suppliers funded and hot
other_moves.detail: We fund lagging suppliers and keep them running above our rate, and we hold buffers [BX-1243, B-2330, B-2043]. Priorities: (1) engines, since LEAP-1B is the 737's sole source and engines have bound the line before [B-1449]; (2) any supplier flagged on the supplier-shortages KPI [B-2283]. The ladder: embed staff, buffer, requalify, fund, acquire. With Spirit in-house since December 2025 [BG-0064], we control the 737 fuselage.

other_moves.move: Balance sheet first in capital allocation
other_moves.detail: Debt repair stays first [BX-1305, BX-0556]. I recommend to the Board no shareholder returns and no new equity until we are solidly investment grade; the Board reserves both decisions. The $10B of undrawn revolvers stays undrawn.

other_moves.move: Stage-gated governance of the launch
other_moves.detail: Before the full Board votes, the Aerospace Safety Committee reviews the launch with the Chief Engineer's readiness view. After launch, each development stage gate is KPI-based, with no subjectivity [BX-1259]. If the plan has to move, we reset it once, conservatively, never in serial slips [BX-1318, BX-1321]. No launched programme is ever cancelled (H5).

other_moves.move: Workforce: retain, train before we build, hire in stages
other_moves.detail: One enterprise retention incentive [BX-1314]. We train before we build [BX-1258]. Engineering hiring is staged toward a peak around 2038-39, since the risk case prices talent poaching and supply-chain bottlenecks at 5 pp for 5 years from EIS.

other_moves.move: 737 MAX and 787 customer commitment
other_moves.detail: Production stability on the 737 MAX and 787 lines comes first, gated by KPIs. The new airplane is built for commonality with the 737 fleet so that our customers' transition is planned, not forced [BX-1273, BX-1274].

decision.public_statement:
We said we'd do a new airplane when the market, the technology and Boeing were all ready. We've done the work to get here: the development programmes we had in front of us are done, and the balance sheet is back where it belongs. So today we are launching a new Boeing single-aisle airplane.

We're planning for entry into service in 2040, and that plan has headroom built into it. It is so much more important that we do this right than fast. We won't build airplanes ahead of a mature design. We'll work the certification plan with the FAA from day one. We'll develop this airplane with our suppliers on cost-plus and risk-share terms, not fixed price.

On engines, we've asked CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce to bring us their best. CFM is our baseline, and we want more than one source of supply on this airplane.

Our 737 MAX and 787 customers come first while we do this. Stable production and the KPIs decide our rates. Debt stays first in our capital allocation. I'm not going to give you any more dates today. The financials will follow our production performance. We still have a lot of work to do.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: fps launch_10yr with fps_engine_code 7; rate_737 hold; re787 hold. This is the plan I framed (plan B), and both test memos recommend it.

1. MY RULINGS ON H1 AND H3 FOR 2030, IN WRITING, WITH EVIDENCE.
- H1 (no fps in Round 1) is LIFTED for 2030. Its 2026 grounds were the unfinished 777X and MAX 7/10 and an unrepaired balance sheet [B-2326, BX-1305], and all of them have closed:
  - the 777X was reset to first delivery in 2027 [BX-0550] and turns cash-positive from 2029 [BX-0547];
  - MAX 7/10 certification was expected in 2026 [BX-1873]. The brief reports no certification trouble, so I treat both as done (inference);
  - debt repair is complete on the GM's tracker: net debt reaches $0 at end-2029 (base) and end-2030 (stress), with no new programme;
  - in July 2026 I said we needed about two more years to be financially ready, with a launch expected around 2029-2030 [BG-0068];
  - the three work streams have converged [B-2303, BX-1296]. Market: the narrowbody demand is there, and Do Nothing loses $3.64-6.26B if Airbus moves. Boeing: finances repaired, and Pope confirms engineering can carry one clean-sheet development. Technology: GTF2 and UltraFan NB, if launched on selection, are ready in 2036 and 2037, and CFM is always ready.
  - The lift is conditional, and every condition has passed: Malave's buffer and fundability tests and Pope's readiness results.
- H3, first half (no 787 Re-engine in Round 1) no longer binds as a hard rule. Its ground was "the 777X comes first" [B-2276], and that has closed. I still HOLD the Re-engine on four grounds:
  - the Board's -$1B Downside limit: it adds -3.58 in S3 and S4;
  - my one-development-at-a-time rule [BX-1239];
  - company doctrine (profile §11.4: keep the 787 a cash source, no Re-engine before 2036);
  - the premium: holding it costs $0 in my expected column.
  H3's second half, H4, H5, H6 and H8 apply as written. H2 cannot bind (earliest EIS 2037). H7 has no trigger: the brief reports no certification trouble.

2. THE TEAM RULE.
- Malave's buffer test (slip leg = S5, the brief's Risk case; floor = Do Nothing's -3.64 less $2B = -5.64):
  - plan B passes at -0.78, $4.86B above the floor;
  - every via-Embraer row fails ($11.83-13.94B below the floor). That veto binds and I accept it.
- Pope's KPI veto does not bind: the brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. It is moot anyway, since I hold the rate.
- Everything else is my call.

3. THE GRID. Board items are the fps launch and the engine code that rides with it. rate_737 and re787 sit at their default (hold).

| Plan | S1 | S2 | S3 | S4 (expected) | S5 (risk case) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Submitted: fps 10-yr + 787 hold | +3.50 | +0.66 | +0.88 | -1.96 | -0.78 |
| Same with fps at its default (Do Nothing) | 0.00 | -3.64 | -2.62 | -6.26 | -3.64 |
| Value of the launch | +3.50 | +4.30 | +3.50 | +4.30 | +2.86 |

- The launch beats Do Nothing by more than ε in every column, so debt-first passes. The grid already nets the discounted debt penalty; I do not subtract it again. Undiscounted, for scale only: 10-year $19.1B, 7-year $22.0B, via Embraer $52.5B.
- Worst column: -1.96 (S4). In no column does the item lose more than $1B against its default.

4. RAMP: 10-YEAR OVER 7-YEAR.
- Against the 7-year the 10-year is +1.30 / -0.46 / +1.30 / -0.46 / +0.05. It is ahead in three columns, more than ε ahead in two, and behind only by 0.46 in S2 and S4, inside ε. Its mean across the five columns is +0.46 against the 7-year's +0.11.
- In my expected S4 the 7-year is the best grid plan by $0.46B. That is a tie, and the team rule breaks it on doing less, better [BX-1239] and the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548]. Both point to the 10-year:
  - a $4.68B smaller bill and $2.9B less undiscounted debt penalty;
  - a 2036 cash peak of about $8.4B against about $12.5B in 2034;
  - every debt line kept, the stress case included (peak $0.0B). The 7-year borrows $0.7B under stress and is still above zero at the 2035 hold year;
  - three years of headroom against our clean-sheet slip record (787-8: May 2008 to September 2011 [B-0031, B-0526]), and no production-certification concurrency [BX-1263], which is my red line.
- The 7-year's S2/S4 edge and its incumbency in 2040 both exist only if it meets NGSA's 2037 EIS to the year. A three-year slip turns it into the 10-year airplane with a bigger bill. Airbus's timeline does not set our date [B-2313].
- Doctrine also points to the 10-year ramp: profile §11.4, "Ramp-up speed: the 10-year ramp".

5. OBJECTIVE LEDGER (Control's mission; it never changes the payoff).
- Debt: plan B reads 2029 / yes / yes ($0.0B) in every column. The 7-year misses the stress line in every column.
- Incumbency, by my sketch of the public share rules:
  - the 10-year holds 40% or more throughout in S1 and S3, but dips to about 37% in 2040 in S2 and S4 (about 32% in S5). It recovers to about 42% by 2045 and about 47% by 2050 on the 3-year lead rule;
  - the 7-year holds in S1-S4 and dips to about 38% in 2040 in S5.
- In every column the 10-year misses no more objectives than the 7-year: S2/S4 trade one miss for one, and in S1, S3 and S5 the 7-year misses more.
- 50/50 is out of reach for every plan.
- I weigh debt, which is on my own ranked list [BX-1305], above an incumbency gain that depends on a schedule our record says we would not hold.

6. 787 RE-ENGINE: hold.
- It adds +2.20 in S1, S2 and S5 and -3.58 in S3 and S4. That is a bet on an A350 choice we cannot see, and it fails the Board's -$1B Downside limit.
- In S4 holding it costs nothing.
- The cost I accept, unpriced: on the 10-year a 2035 Re-engine would overlap 5 years and break H4, so the next H4-legal round is 2045. Widebody growth comes from Charleston capacity [BX-1317], and the 787 stays a cash source. Doctrine, not my record, drives this.

7. RATE INCREASE: hold.
- It adds -0.74 in every column beside the launch, so it fails its business case. Its +2.30 alone needs fps on hold and S1 or S3, and even then it assumes neither new narrowbody is ever launched.
- This is the only round the board offers it, so the deferral is a loss I accept, not a wait.
- It is not a reply to anyone (H6).

8. ENGINE CODE 7: costs nothing on the board.
- On today's record the fitted source at a 2040 EIS is CFM (1).
- If P&W (GTF2, ready 2036) and Rolls-Royce (UltraFan NB, ready 2037) launch on selection this round, both are ready 4 and 3 years before EIS: three sources by 2050 and three narrowbody engine makers.
- Code 7 is in no disallowed pair. Doctrine and my Low-confidence lean were code 3; code 7 keeps CFM as the fallback and serves the supply-stability enabler.

9. PREMIUM (H8): $0.46B, logged.
- What it is: the 10-year against the best S4 plan (7-year), counted in S2 and S4.
- Why: doctrine (higher-confidence plan with headroom, doing less, no concurrency) plus objective (the stress-case debt line).
- Re-engine hold $0, rate hold $0, code $0. Total $0.46B, $1.54B inside the cap.
- What would break it: an expected column of S1, S2 or S5, where the Re-engine hold would read $2.20B. In that case the hold rests on the Board's veto and H-rules, not on doctrine.

10. DEBT PATH, plan B (Malave's reconstruction, matching the brief's cells within $0.05B):
- base net debt $16.5B (2027), $6.7B (2028), $0 every year from 2029;
- stress $18.3B, $11.7B, $3.3B, then $0 from 2030, with at least $2.5B of headroom (2036);
- programme cash: about $3.0B in 2030, rising to about $8.4B in 2036;
- no new equity and no shareholder return in the plan.

airbus.public_statement: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. On that basis, Airbus is launching its next-generation single-aisle aircraft. We prepared it through a decade of technology roadmaps, and we are launching it now because those technologies are mature, not to meet anyone else's calendar. We target entry into service in the second half of the 2030s. Customers have been well served by a choice of engines on the A320 family, and the same will apply to its successor. We have selected CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce, and we invite all three to join the programme as risk-sharing partners. Until the new aircraft enters service, the A320neo and A350 families remain our priority, with a disciplined and controlled production ramp-up and continued work to secure our supply chain, engines and critical materials first. We will fund the programme with financial discipline, as disciplined investments in preparing our future portfolio, within our financial flexibility and our existing shareholder return policy. We will continue to work with our industry partners for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero regime for aerospace trade. A stronger and more sovereign European aerospace industry is built on one well-prepared programme at a time.
airbus.rationale:
QUESTION. 2030 is the last year of the 2028-2030 launch window. Do we launch NGSA on its technology clock, alone, with an engine code that rebuilds our engine-supply base, as one clean Board item?

STEP 1: DELETE RED LINES AND FIVE-PILLARS FAILURES.
- All six Delay Tactics rows are deleted under rule 4. Boeing has not launched fps on the public record, so any move would be naked and draw the $48.32B fine. 'both' is a second move. bottleneck is an integrity flag. Toepfer and Wagner both fail them, and the Board would veto them.
- NGSA + A350 Re-engine (+47.57 / +25.11 / +19.03 / +25.11 / +42.81 / +20.36) is deleted under rule 6. It is two new launches in one round with a 5-year overlap, and the $1B exception fails in S5 and S6 (-2.15).

STEP 2: SURVIVORS AGAINST THE TWO TESTS.
- NGSA hold + A350 hold (0.00 / -3.30 / -4.99 / -3.30 / -0.86 / -4.16) fails both. Toepfer's robustness test fails, Wagner's production-readiness test fails because the plan misses the window, and my NGSA clock test fails.
- NGSA hold + A350 Re-engine (+3.26 / -0.05 / -1.74 / -0.05 / -1.50 / -4.80) also fails both: Toepfer's robustness test (worst column S6 at -4.80) and Wagner's A350F/Spirit-absorption and production-readiness tests.
- NGSA launch + A350 hold + Delay Tactics none (+45.82 / +23.37 / +17.28 / +23.37 / +44.96 / +22.51) passes every test of both men. It is the only survivor, and it is also the company default.

STEP 3: CHOICE.
- Expected scenario: S1, rivals hold. In S1 the best grid plan is the deleted NGSA + A350 Re-engine row, $1.75B above the default. A red line is not traded for PV, so that gap is recorded, not paid for. The survivor is chosen.
- No other survivor lies within $1B, so the tie-breaks do not apply. The plan already scores on all five of them: no early EIS, no concurrency, the last possible capex start inside the window, EIS 2037 holding within 2035-2037, and one Board item.

cfo.memo:
Board paper, round 2030: NGSA launch. CFO test result: pass.

Liquidity. NGSA costs $35.52B over 2030-2036: $5.07B a year, against one year's free cash flow of €4,753m, about $5.2B at an assumed $1.10 [AX-0104]. Headroom: $0.13B. Nothing may run alongside it. An A350 Re-engine adds $1.0B plus $0.6B strain, for $6.67B a year. One Delay Tactics move adds $0.10-0.14B a year, which uses up the headroom, and with no fps on the record it risks a $48.32B fine, 3.6 times net cash.

Robustness. The worst plausible column is S3, at +17.28. The NGSA item gains $22.27-45.82B in every column, which clears the Board's $2B limit.

Balance sheet. On the FY2025 base the margin is thin: NGSA would take 97% of a year's cash, and the dividend would draw on net cash. On the 2030 run-rate in the bank models (€10.7-11.6bn of FCF), NGSA takes 40-43%. The 30-50% payout then stays fundable, with no equity raise and no dividend cut [AG-0058]. The €5bn buyback runs 2026-2029, before the spend [AG-0059]. Present the launch as "disciplined investments in preparing its future portfolio" [AX-0012], inside the stated range. On the board's books the bill lands in 2037 as one $35.52B charge.

Not fundable: NGSA plus an A350 Re-engine (rule 6, $6.67B a year, -2.15 in S5 and S6) and any Delay Tactics. An A350 Re-engine first passes in 2045.

One Board item: ngsa: launch, by Qualified Majority. On the engine code I defer to Lars and expect code 7.

ops.memo:
Role-derived tests, Very low confidence: nothing of mine is on record.

Pass: launch NGSA now, alone. 2030 closes the 2028-2030 window; EIS 2037 sits behind the 2035 technology-ready year. One programme: zero overlap, zero strain. The end-2027 rate date has passed and the brief reports no ramp, supply or quality problem. No five-pillars flag.

Engine code 7. CFM is the anchor and certifies first; P&W and Rolls-Royce are named. Ready by 2037: CFM always; GTF2 in 2036 if launched now; UltraFan NB in 2037, zero margin. Only this round can trigger them. Without them NGSA flies CFM alone, and in 2050 our narrowbody is single-source, the exposure that slipped our ramp [AX-0054]. Unpriced: three integrations and certifications on the same engineering teams, and a zero-margin UltraFan. Certify in sequence, as on the A320neo, and drop any maker off track at the 2035 review. Avoid codes 1, 2 and 4: a non-CFM single source.

Fail, binding: an A350 Re-engine this round. Five-year overlap, $3B strain, A350F and Spirit packages still being absorbed, and a second launch in one round (rule 6). +1.75 in S1 becomes -2.15 in S5-S6. My capacity test first passes in 2035, at the two-year limit ($1.2B strain); cash is Thomas's call.

Fail, binding: any Delay Tactics. No fps on record, so any move is naked.

Neither veto rests on safety, quality or the ramp; both rest on red lines. Add the engine-maker invitation and our own supply moves.

other_moves.detail: Continue to bring critical work packages in-house and to de-risk titanium and rare earths for our own production system [AX-0060, AX-0061, AX-0062, AX-0063]. This is aimed only at our own disciplined and controlled ramp-up. It is not aimed at any rival's supply chain.

other_moves.detail: Keep code 7 unless the 2035 bulletin shows that P&W or Rolls-Royce has not launched, or has an engine that is off track for a 2037 entry into service. In that case, remove that maker only. The change is never made in reaction to Boeing.

If ramp cash stays near the FY2025 level, returns are kept at the lower end of the range in 2030-2036 rather than drawing on net cash. The $35.52B programme charge at entry into service is reported beside the cash view. No internal long-term-plan targets are disclosed.

other_moves.move: Zero-for-zero trade advocacy through industry coalitions

decision.public_statement: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. On that basis, Airbus is launching its next-generation single-aisle aircraft. We prepared it through a decade of technology roadmaps, and we are launching it now because those technologies are mature, not to meet anyone else's calendar. We target entry into service in the second half of the 2030s. Customers have been well served by a choice of engines on the A320 family, and the same will apply to its successor. We have selected CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce, and we invite all three to join the programme as risk-sharing partners. Until the new aircraft enters service, the A320neo and A350 families remain our priority, with a disciplined and controlled production ramp-up and continued work to secure our supply chain, engines and critical materials first. We will fund the programme with financial discipline, as disciplined investments in preparing our future portfolio, within our financial flexibility and our existing shareholder return policy. We will continue to work with our industry partners for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero regime for aerospace trade. A stronger and more sovereign European aerospace industry is built on one well-prepared programme at a time.
decision.rationale:
QUESTION. 2030 is the last year of the 2028-2030 launch window. Do we launch NGSA on its technology clock, alone, with an engine code that rebuilds our engine-supply base, as one clean Board item?

STEP 1: DELETE RED LINES AND FIVE-PILLARS FAILURES.
- All six Delay Tactics rows are deleted under rule 4. Boeing has not launched fps on the public record, so any move would be naked and draw the $48.32B fine. 'both' is a second move. bottleneck is an integrity flag. Toepfer and Wagner both fail them, and the Board would veto them.
- NGSA + A350 Re-engine (+47.57 / +25.11 / +19.03 / +25.11 / +42.81 / +20.36) is deleted under rule 6. It is two new launches in one round with a 5-year overlap, and the $1B exception fails in S5 and S6 (-2.15).

STEP 2: SURVIVORS AGAINST THE TWO TESTS.
- NGSA hold + A350 hold (0.00 / -3.30 / -4.99 / -3.30 / -0.86 / -4.16) fails both. Toepfer's robustness test fails, Wagner's production-readiness test fails because the plan misses the window, and my NGSA clock test fails.
- NGSA hold + A350 Re-engine (+3.26 / -0.05 / -1.74 / -0.05 / -1.50 / -4.80) also fails both: Toepfer's robustness test (worst column S6 at -4.80) and Wagner's A350F/Spirit-absorption and production-readiness tests.
- NGSA launch + A350 hold + Delay Tactics none (+45.82 / +23.37 / +17.28 / +23.37 / +44.96 / +22.51) passes every test of both men. It is the only survivor, and it is also the company default.

STEP 3: CHOICE.
- Expected scenario: S1, rivals hold. In S1 the best grid plan is the deleted NGSA + A350 Re-engine row, $1.75B above the default. A red line is not traded for PV, so that gap is recorded, not paid for. The survivor is chosen.
- No other survivor lies within $1B, so the tie-breaks do not apply. The plan already scores on all five of them: no early EIS, no concurrency, the last possible capex start inside the window, EIS 2037 holding within 2035-2037, and one Board item.
- Robustness: the worst plausible column is S3 (fps 7-yr, EIS 2037, the same year as NGSA) at +17.28, positive. The decision is identical in every column. Nothing here is timed around Boeing.

STEP 4: OVERRIDES. None. No soft veto stands against the chosen plan. The override budget (one per game) is untouched.

ENGINE CODE: 7 (CFM, P&W, Rolls-Royce). This is Wagner's supply recommendation, taken as my agent file directs, and the Board's preferred code.
- It keeps CFM as the anchor and appears in no barred pair, so Boeing's code choice cannot force a change.
- It is the only code that can reach 3 sources / 3 makers in 2050. Without it, or if both makers hold, NGSA flies CFM alone (1 / 1).
- Only this round can trigger GTF2 (ready 2036) and UltraFan NB (ready 2037) in time for entry into service.
- On this board an unready maker is dropped, so the code carries no EIS risk and no payoff effect.
- Unpriced load: three engine integrations and certifications. It is mitigated by certifying in sequence with CFM first and by reviewing the code in 2035, only to remove a maker that has not launched or is off track.

BOARD-GATE LINE (one item: ngsa: launch, Qualified Majority; the engine code rides with it).
- Five pillars: pass. Nothing is covert and no flag was raised by Toepfer (Internal Control) or by Wagner.
- Toepfer's test: pass. Peak programme cash is $35.52B / 7 = $5.07B a year in 2030-2036 against $5.2B, with $0.13B headroom and no concurrent programme. Net cash and the A+/A1 rating hold with no new debt or equity. On the 2030 run-rate the payout stays inside 30-50%. On the board's books the $35.52B lands at EIS in 2037, and that charge is reported beside the cash view.
- Wagner's test: pass. Safety and quality pass, the A320 ramp shield passes, A350F absorption is untouched, and overlap and strain are both zero.
- Grid ΔPV: the item against hold is +45.82 / +26.67 / +22.27 / +26.67 / +45.82 / +26.67, a gain in every column. The plan row is +45.82 / +23.37 / +17.28 / +23.37 / +44.96 / +22.51, worst column S3 at +17.28.
- The item clears the Board's downside test (no loss in any column against a $2B limit), its liquidity test and its technology-clock test (EIS 2037, not before 2035).
- rea350 hold and delay_tactics none are defaults, not items.

DELAY TACTICS: none. The team's stricter condition (the move must change who enters service first) stands. I do not set it aside. Delay Tactics will never appear in any public line.

A350 RE-ENGINE: on hold.
- Wagner's capacity test would first pass in 2035, at the 2-year overlap limit.
- Toepfer's peak-cash line moves the first passing round to 2045 on these bills (a 2035 launch runs at $6.67B a year in 2035-2036).
- It never comes after a 787 Re-engine (rule 3).

RECORD. Ordering principle in my framing: pillars, then ramp, then preparing the Airbus of the 30s, then whether the Board can take it [AX-0073, AX-0081, AX-0020, A-0409, AX-0026, AX-0010, AX-0054]. Confidence in my decision style is Low; the procedure follows the team rule and profile.md §9.

memo_weighing.cfo:
Toepfer's tests are role-derived (Low confidence).

On option 1 every test passes: peak cash ($5.07B vs $5.2B, $0.13B headroom), robustness (worst column S3 +17.28; NGSA item +22.27 to +45.82), overlap and one launch (zero overlap), five pillars and integrity (no flag), net cash/rating/payout on the 2030 run-rate, and Board items (one, by Qualified Majority).

His vetoes on the other options are binding and accepted:
- Option 3 rests on red-line rule 6, plus peak cash of $6.67B and -2.15 in S5 and S6.
- Option 5 rests on red-line rule 4 and the $48.32B naked-fine exposure.
- Options 2 and 4 rest on robustness. Neither is within reach of a $1B override, since they trail option 1 by $19-46B.

Accepted as corrections and conditions:
- One Delay Tactics move adds $0.10-0.14B a year, not $6.67B, and uses up the headroom. The real exposure is the fine. My framing overstated this.
- On the FY2025 base, the dividend would draw on net cash. This becomes a payout guardrail: stay inside 30-50%, at the lower end if ramp cash does not arrive. NGSA itself stays (rule 7).
- The $35.52B charge at the 2037 EIS is reported beside the cash view.
- The first passing round for an A350 Re-engine is 2045 on these bills.

On the engine code he defers to Wagner. No override.
memo_weighing.ops:
Wagner's tests are role-derived (Very low confidence).

On option 1 every test passes: five pillars and quality, A320 ramp shield, engineering capacity (zero overlap), production readiness (last year of the window, EIS 2037), and A350F/Spirit absorption (rea350 hold). His engine-code recommendation (code 7) is a supply recommendation, not a veto ground. I took it as my agent file directs, together with his mitigations: sequential certification with CFM as anchor, and a 2035 review only to remove a maker that has not launched or is off track.

His vetoes on options 3, 4, 5 and 2 are binding and accepted. As he states, none rests on safety, quality or the A320 ramp. They rest on red lines (rules 6 and 4) and on his soft tests (capacity, A350F absorption, production readiness), which no plan within $1B could override.

His note that his capacity test would pass an A350 Re-engine in 2035 at the 2-year limit is recorded. Toepfer's cash line governs and points to 2045. No override.

decision.expected_scenario: S1: rivals hold. Boeing has said a new aircraft comes 'not before 2035' and is still repairing its balance sheet, and the bulletin records no launch. S2 and S4 (fps 10-yr or via Embraer, EIS 2040) are close behind. The worst plausible column is S3 (fps 7-yr, EIS 2037, the same year as NGSA), where the plan still returns +17.28. The order is the same in every column.
decision.best_grid_plan_in_expected_scenario: NGSA + A350 Re-engine at +47.57 in S1. It is deleted for a company red line: rule 6, two new launches in one round with a 5-year overlap and -2.15 in S5 and S6. It also fails Toepfer's peak-cash test ($6.67B vs $5.2B) and Wagner's capacity and A350F tests, and the Board would veto it. The best surviving plan is NGSA + A350: hold + Delay Tactics none at +45.82 in S1. That is the company default and the plan ordered.
decision.premium_reason: No premium is paid. The only higher row in S1 (NGSA + A350 Re-engine, +$1.75B) breaks red-line rule 6 and is deleted before the doctrine-default comparison, so the $1.75B is recorded, not paid as a premium. The chosen plan is the best surviving plan in every column bar the deleted ones. No PV is traded for the briefing goal or the engine-supply enabler: the engine code is payoff-neutral on this board, and holding NGSA to keep 2 / 2 engine sources would cost $22.27-45.82B, far beyond any premium allowed.
decision.objective_note:
The briefing goal (Defend the 60/40 edge; Protect the A320 family; Enabler: stable engine supply) is scored by the GM and does not change the payoff. No PV was traded for it.

Defend 60/40. Met today. With NGSA launched it is met in S1 and S5: NGSA alone gains 3 pp a year from 2037, to the cap. My reading of rules.md, not tabulated in the brief, for the fps columns:
- S2, S4 and S6 (fps EIS 2040): NGSA leads by 3 years, which points to roughly 53% in the long run. 2040 holds above 60%, but 2045 and 2050 fall below.
- S3 (same EIS): we drift toward 50%.
- In every fps column, holding NGSA does worse, so the launch is also the plan that best defends the edge.

Protect the A320 family. Met in every column: nothing moves before 2037 and no Rate Increase is on record.

Enabler, dual or triple sources. Met today (CFM + P&W GTF). With NGSA it falls to 1 / 1 in 2050 if P&W and Rolls-Royce hold, and rises to 3 / 3 if both launch when selected. Code 7 is the only code that can reach 3 / 3, and this is the only round in which it can be triggered.

Enabler, three narrowbody makers. Not met today. It becomes met only if Rolls-Royce brings an NB engine (UltraFan NB, or the Joint Venture engine) that is ready by 2037. Code 7 plus the public risk-sharing invitation is the most I can do without trading PV.
decision.predictions:
Boeing in 2030: most likely holds (S1, about 45%). Next most likely is an fps 10-yr or via Embraer (S2/S4, about 30% together), then an fps 7-yr (S3, about 10%) and a 787 Re-engine with or without fps (S5/S6, about 15%). A 737 Rate Increase is possible but would not change our programmes. Probability-weighted ΔPV on these weights is about +33.9B; in S1 it is +45.82B.

P&W: likely to answer our selection with GTF2 launch_if_selected, ready 2036 with one year of margin, so that it keeps its place on our narrowbody. A Joint Venture commitment with Rolls-Royce is possible.

Rolls-Royce: less certain. UltraFan NB launched now has zero margin to a 2037 entry into service. It may prefer the Joint Venture (ready 2036, counted as one source) or stay on widebody moves.

CFM: likely to launch a ducted engine or rely on a LEAP derivative. It is fitted on NGSA either way.

Board: approves ngsa: launch by Qualified Majority with code 7, and vetoes nothing in this package.

2035 bulletin: NGSA in development with engine-ready dates published. At the 2035 round the code is reviewed only to remove a maker that has not launched. NGSA is not re-timed for any Boeing move. The A350 Re-engine stays on hold on current bills (first passing round 2045, never after a 787 Re-engine).
