I re-tested Faury's final orders, not the frame: ngsa launch, ngsa_engine_code 7, rea350 hold, delay_tactics none. They are the same as my recommended orders.

Peak cash: pass. NGSA costs $35.52B / 7 = $5.07B a year in 2030-2036. One year's FCF is €4,753m x $1.10 = $5.23B, which I round to $5.2B [AX-0104]. Headroom is $0.13B, or $0.15B against the unrounded figure. Nothing else runs in those years: no strain, no A350 Re-engine, no Delay Tactics.

Robustness: pass. I checked the plan row against the brief: +45.82 / +23.37 / +17.28 / +23.37 / +44.96 / +22.51. The worst plausible column is S3 at +17.28. The NGSA item against hold gains +22.27 to +45.82 in every column, well inside the Board's $2B downside limit [AX-0022].

Overlap and the one-launch rule (rule 6): pass, with one launch and zero overlap [A-0343, A-0401]. Fine exposure, second move and poaching do not apply, since no move is ordered. Faury records that the team's stricter Delay Tactics condition stands.

Five pillars: no flag. The supply-security move is limited to our own ramp. The trade advocacy and the risk-sharing invitation are public and unpriced. I could defend all of it to the Audit Committee [AX-0073, AX-0106].

Overrides: none used and none needed, so the one-per-game budget is untouched. One Board item: ngsa: launch, by Qualified Majority [AX-0026, AG-0049].

My conditions are carried into the decision:
- shareholder returns stay inside the 30-50% payout range, at the lower end if ramp cash does not arrive;
- the $35.52B charge at the 2037 EIS is reported beside the cash view;
- no long-term-plan targets are disclosed [AX-0005];
- the public statement goes to the Board with the package [AX-0004].

Watch items, not vetoes: with $0.13B of headroom, any added programme cash in 2030-2036 needs a fresh peak-cash test. NGSA alone fails if its bill goes above $36.4B, FCF falls below €4.61bn, or the rate drops below $1.068 per €.

On the engine code I defer to Lars Wagner. It does not change our payoff on the board.

ops.note:
Veto check, round 1 (2030). Lars Wagner, CEO Commercial Aircraft. My tests are derived from my role, not from my own record, so confidence is Very low.

I concur. The orders match my recommendation exactly: ngsa launch, ngsa_engine_code 7, rea350 hold, delay_tactics none.

How the orders fare on my tests:
- **Five pillars and quality: pass.** Every order is public and nothing is covert. The statement opens with safety and quality and gives a window for entry into service, not a date. The brief reports no quality event.
- **A320 ramp shield: pass.** 2030 is after the end-2027 rate date. NB deliveries are flat at 1,200 a year (60.0%), and the brief reports no ramp or supply problem.
- **Engineering capacity: pass.** NGSA is the only programme, so overlap is 0 years and strain is $0.
- **Production readiness: pass.** 2030 is the last year of the 2028-2030 window. EIS is 2037, after the 2035 technology-ready year.
- **A350F and Spirit absorption: pass.** rea350 is on hold, so nothing competes with the A350F or the Spirit A350 work packages.
- **Supply crunch, engine maturity slip and Boeing Rate Increase: not applicable.** The brief reports none of them.

**Company red lines: no breach.**
- Rule 1: EIS 2037 is not before 2035.
- Rule 4: no Delay Tactics move is ordered.
- Rule 5: no poaching is ordered.
- Rule 6: there is one new launch this round and no overlap.

**Overrides.** None was used and none was needed, so the one-per-game override is still unused. No Delay Tactics move was ordered, and Faury records that the team's stricter condition stands.

**Engine code 7: my recommendation, adopted.** CFM stays the anchor, and code 7 is in no barred pair under rules.md. Only this round can trigger P&W GTF2 (ready 2036) and Rolls-Royce UltraFan NB (ready 2037, no margin) in time for NGSA. If both launch, we have 3 engine sources and 3 makers in 2050. If both hold, NGSA flies CFM alone, with 1 source and 1 maker in 2050.

The three mitigations I asked for are in other_moves:
- certify the engines one after another, with CFM first;
- review the code in 2035, only to remove a maker that has not launched or is off track, and never in reaction to Boeing;
- secure supply for our own ramp only, not aimed at any rival's supply chain.

**One wording note, not a veto.** The public line "the same will apply to its successor", on engine choice, only holds if P&W or Rolls-Royce actually launch an engine. If both hold, NGSA has one engine source. To protect the credibility of what we say in public, I would soften it to "we intend to offer a choice of engines" before release. This is Faury's call, and it does not touch safety, quality or the five pillars.

Evidence: AX-0073, AX-0054, AX-0082, AX-0060, A-0441, A-0225, A-0366, A-0243, A-0360.

items.ground:
The Board approves this Qualified Majority item, a programme launch above EUR 800m, on the following record. The Board checked the brief's grid itself.
- Unresolved objection: pass. Both veto checks concur, neither reports a red-line breach, there are no overrides and there is no revision. Wagner's wording note is not a veto.
- Override review: not engaged. No override was used.
- Liquidity and rating: pass, narrowly. $35.52B / 7 = $5.07B a year in 2030-2036 against the $5.2B line (EUR 4,753m at $1.10), with $0.13B of headroom and nothing running alongside. No new debt and no equity raise.
- One clean sheet: pass. One launch this round, with zero overlap and zero strain.
- Technology clock: pass. EIS 2030 + 7 = 2037, not before 2035, in the last year of the 2028-2030 window.
- Downside: pass. The item value (the 'NGSA + A350: hold' row minus 'hold + hold') is +45.82 / +26.67 / +22.27 / +26.67 / +45.82 / +26.67 across S1-S6. It gains in the CEO's expected column, S1, and in every column the bulletin leaves open. The plan's worst column is S3 at +17.28.
- Integrity: pass. Nothing is covert and Delay Tactics are none.
- Safety and ramp: pass. Wagner passes the five pillars, quality, the A320 ramp shield, production readiness and A350F/Spirit absorption, and reports no supply crunch.
- Returns kept fundable: passes through Liquidity. The CFO's FY2025-base caveat is taken up below as a recommendation. Under the plan-level rule it could never be a ground against NGSA on its clock.
- Engine supply: code 7 keeps CFM and names a second and a third maker. It is in no barred pair. It is not a veto ground.
acceptable_alternatives: launch with any engine code (the Board never vetoes a code on its own)
hold (the default; the Board would not veto it, but recommends against missing the window)

recommendations.text: Liquidity has only $0.13B of headroom. Any programme cash added in 2030-2036, of whatever kind, must come back to the Board with a fresh year-by-year peak-cash test. The CFO's break-evens should be watched at each round and reported when crossed: an NGSA bill above $36.4B, FCF below EUR 4.61bn, or a rate below $1.068 per EUR.

Public statement: the Board supports Wagner's note. Replace 'the same will apply to its successor' with 'we intend to offer a choice of engines'. A second source depends on decisions by P&W and Rolls-Royce that Airbus does not control. Keep entry into service as 'the second half of the 2030s', with no dates or internal targets and nothing on Delay Tactics. The engine-maker invitation remains an unpriced, public other_move.

Engine supply:
- Keep code 7, with CFM as the anchor and certifying first, and the other makers certified in sequence.
- Review the code in 2035 only to remove a maker that has not launched or is off track for 2037, never in reaction to Boeing.
- If neither P&W nor Rolls-Royce launches this round, NGSA will be single-source in 2050 (1 source / 1 maker). The ExCo should then report in 2035 how supply resilience is protected, without trading PV.
- Wagner should report the integration and certification load of up to three engines at the Board's twice-yearly safety review.

Securing our own supply (in-house work packages, titanium, rare earths) must stay confined to Airbus's own ramp and never become a first claim aimed at a rival's supply chain. The Board asks that the Ethics, Compliance and Sustainability Committee be informed of these moves.

One programme at a time: keep the A350 Re-engine on hold. On these bills, a 2035 launch overlaps NGSA in 2035-2036 at about $6.67B a year and fails Liquidity, so 2045 is the first passing round. Bring it back only with fresh peak-cash arithmetic if the bills change, and never after a Boeing 787 Re-engine.

Delay Tactics stay off, and the team's stricter condition stands. Bottleneck and both are never acceptable. Poaching may come to the Board only once Boeing's fps launch is on the public record, fps is not in service, NGSA is in development, and every integrity condition holds.

Reaction discipline: NGSA stays on its own clock. It is not to be accelerated, delayed or cancelled for any Boeing move. A cancellation would need continuing to lose at least $1B against cancelling in every plausible column. In 2035, read Boeing only from the bulletin, and show the worst plausible column again together with the 60/40 path by column.

board_review.note: The Board approves the one Board item: ngsa: launch in 2030 with engine code 7, by Qualified Majority. EIS 2037 respects the technology clock and uses the last year of the window. On the brief's grid the item gains in every column (+22.27 to +45.82), so it clears the Downside test. Peak cash is $5.07B against the $5.2B line, a pass but a narrow one. The ExCo raises no objection, uses no override and has no safety, quality or ramp failure on record. A350 hold and Delay Tactics none are defaults and are not reviewed. The Board's main caution is the balance sheet. The headroom is $0.13B, and on the FY2025 base the dividend would draw on net cash. The Board therefore asks for a net-cash bridge and for the payout guardrail to be confirmed. It also asks that the engine-choice line be softened to 'we intend to offer a choice of engines'.

other_moves.move: Offer a CFM engine to every airframer on every new narrowbody
other_moves.detail: This is H1: we refuse no airframer and lock none out [CX-0587, CX-0185]. The offer is a LEAP derivative or the new ducted engine, as each customer chooses. No price or terms are stated in public: CFM narrowbody pricing is a joint decision with Safran [CX-0184].

other_moves.move: CFM partner consultation on the Ducted and Embraer launches
other_moves.detail: Both CFM orders go through CFM governance with Safran. Consent is assumed, with stated reasons. The Ducted keeps both airframers' next aircraft on a CFM engine, and with them the aftermarket the partners split equally. Embraer puts a CFM engine in front of a third airframer, which fits 'serve every airframer'. The record shows no Safran position, so none is asserted. GEnx is GE alone and needs no gate.

other_moves.move: Supply-base readiness for a three-project stack (FLIGHT DECK reviews)
other_moves.detail: Ali's condition is taken up. GEnx upgrade work is paced behind the Ducted's development peak; GEnx counts no earlier than 2042 without a Re-engine. Monthly operating reviews cover the 9 suppliers at 15 sites behind 80% of past shortages [CX-0613]. LEAP OE delivery and spares come first, and spares never crowd out OE [CX-0529]. The trigger to drop Embraer and GEnx is a supply 'no' from Ali on field data.

other_moves.move: Cross-functional design and test gates on the Ducted
other_moves.detail: Every Ducted design and test gate is a cross-functional call, never one person's [CX-0012]. Durability is not traded for fuel burn or schedule [CX-0208]. The 2036 ready year stays inside the company until a turn-on, turn-off test backs it [CX-0009].

other_moves.move: Keep RISE funded as technology and set the gates for the 2035 product call
other_moves.detail: There is no cancel and no 'program dividend' [CX-0174, CX-0214]. Ali's milestones must be in hand by the 2035 round: (1) the ground and flight test done; (2) compact-core durability turned on and off, with the HPT dust testing closed; (3) more than 20% fuel burn shown in engine test, not analysis; (4) noise below today's LEAP. The product call is made in 2035, on the bulletin and these tests.

other_moves.move: Fund the package inside the capital allocation framework
other_moves.detail: The package needs about $1.0B a year of new R&D and strain ($0.67B Ducted plus $0.33B strain) against about $2.5B of room. Returns stay at or above 70% of FCF [CX-0645], and the A-range balance sheet is held. Any unbudgeted spend comes out of buybacks, not the dividend or the rating. That is analyst context only, per Ghai.

cfm.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That doesn't change this year.

Let me tell you what we know and what we don't. Nothing new has launched yet in the narrowbody. When it does, our customers decide the aircraft and the timing, not us, and we don't have a birthright on that next order. So CFM is launching a new ducted engine programme, so that every airframer has a CFM engine to choose on whatever comes next. CFM is also partnering with Embraer, putting a CFM engine in front of a third airframer. And at GE we're launching a GEnx upgrade for the 787 and the airlines that fly it.

RISE remains our next generation. We're all in on the open fan technology, and it stays funded. But it's really not for us to say when that architecture enters service. If an airframer launches a new narrowbody now, the open fan won't be ready for it, and we won't ask anyone to wait.

Here's what we don't know: which aircraft launch, when, and with which engines. We won't give you dates our testing hasn't earned. You'll get them when it has. We'll fund this within our capital allocation framework and keep the balance sheet where it is. We want to be on all the critical platforms that matter in the decades ahead. It's that simple, ain't that hard.
cfm.rationale:
DECISION. Launch the Ducted, Partner Embraer and the GEnx upgrade (upgrade_genx9). Hold the Open Fan and Lobby. Nothing is cancelled. All five orders follow the frame, and both memos recommend the same five.

WHAT GAME, HOW WE WIN [CX-0467]. The game is the installed base on the next narrowbody [CX-0422], not share for its own sake [CX-0493]. Both new narrowbodies, fps and NGSA, are open, and orders are sealed. Hold loses -32.07 to -105.01 in every column where an airframer launches. S3 (NGSA, code 2) and S6 (codes 1 and 2) are the columns where a rival selection takes CFM's slot. "We don't have a birthright on that next order" [CX-0564].

TESTS
(1) Additive and paid for the risk [CX-0301]. The package, Ducted + Partner Embraer + GEnx upgrade, is the best grid plan in S2 to S5: S2 -20.69, S3 -71.86, S4 -50.10, S5 -48.96. Its S1 cost is named: -5.22 against hold, or -6.00 against GEnx alone, which is the $4B bill plus the $2B strain and no more. The risk is worth it because the package is worth +10.61 to +13.05 wherever an airframer launches, and the loss is capped at the bill when none does.

(2) Low case first [CX-0248, CX-0536]. The expected column is S2: Airbus launches NGSA and keeps today's dual-source A320neo pattern (code 6). That is the record's pattern, not a hoped-for selection. S2 sits below S1 for every plan, so it books low.

(3) Hard rule 3. The trigger is the grid's slot-taking columns, because no rival engine is launched, committed or selected on the record. S3 is the column that pays it: the Ducted is worth +10.17 against hold, and the package +13.05 against GEnx alone. S6 names the trigger but does not pay it (-0.49, or -1.38). Ghai accepts the trigger through S3, not S6.

(4) My 20% line, rebutted. The 20% line [CX-0217] binds the next-generation product, which is RISE. The ducted engine has "less than half the fuel burn improvements" of an open fan [CX-0183; Ali, CX-0180]. It cannot meet 20%, and it is not offered as the next generation. It is a defence of the installed base under hard rule 3, and it is never called next-generation in public. The durability line [CX-0208] stands: Ali raises no durability or safety flag, and every design gate is cross-functional [CX-0012].

(5) Supply. Two or more projects draw the $2B strain. The grid pays it in S2 to S5. Ali gives no supply 'no', on condition that GEnx is paced behind the Ducted's peak.

WHY NOW, NOT AFTER THE 2035 BULLETIN. Launched now, the Ducted is ready in 2036 against a 2037 entry (NGSA or a 7-year fps) and a 2040 entry (10-year fps or the Embraer route). Launched in 2035, it is ready only in 2041. Ghai sizes the cost of waiting at about $4.3B in S2 and S3, $4.5B in S5 and $1.1B in S4. Waiting saves $0.49B in S6, and in S1 it saves up to $4.00B. Net edge for launching now: +$1.06B to +$1.26B on my weights, +$0.64B to +$0.88B on his. Waiting wins only once P(S1) passes about 0.45. Ghai's numbers show deferring Embraer or GEnx to 2035 would still draw the strain while the Ducted is in development, so it saves nothing.

THE STACK, AND MY OWN CONDITION MISSED. I said the add-ons had to clear Ducted alone by more than $1B on my weights. They clear it by $0.95B, missing by $0.05B: inside ε. Elsewhere they clear it by +$1.21B in S2, +$1.46B on equal weights and +$0.83B on Ghai's. They lose $1.22B in S1 and $0.11B in S6. So the tie-break decides, "safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order" [CX-0658]:
- Safety: a tie. No flag on either plan.
- Quality: a tie on the evidence. The grid charges the load at $2B, and Ali has no test or field data either way. I don't invent a flag. I take his pacing condition and the supplier watch.
- Delivery: the package wins. It puts a CFM engine in front of a third airframer and keeps the 787 on product (H1: "on all the critical platforms" [CX-0587]).
It is decided at delivery, with cost (+$0.95B weighted, best plan in S2) confirming it. GEnx never sits beside a lone Ducted (-1.22 to -1.23 in every column).

HELD
- Open Fan: launched now it is ready in 2045, the same as a 2035 launch. It waits in every launch column, at -$8.00B to -$57.60B against hold (H2) [CX-0205]. RISE stays whole as technology (H5) [CX-0174, CX-0214].
- Lobby: does nothing without an Open Fan.

BOARD ITEMS, BY COLUMN, S1 / S2 / S3 / S4 / S5 / S6
- Submitted package: -5.22 / -20.69 / -71.86 / -50.10 / -48.96 / -105.61. Against Do Nothing in S2 that is +11.38; the worst column against Do Nothing is S1, at -5.22.
- ducted (package minus GEnx alone, Embraer defaulted with it): -6.00 / +10.61 / +13.05 / +10.17 / +12.85 / -1.38. Weighted +4.96. The worst is S1 at -6.00, equal to its $6B bill.
- partner_embraer (package minus Ducted + GEnx): 0.00 / +2.44 / +4.88 / +3.73 / +3.97 / +1.12. Weighted +2.18. It never goes below zero.
- genx (package minus Ducted + Embraer): +0.78 / +0.78 / +0.78 / +0.77 / +0.77 / +0.78.

SAFRAN GATE (H7, CFM parity rule)
- ducted: consent assumed, because it keeps both airframers' next aircraft on CFM and the aftermarket the partners split equally. A launch ahead of a committed airframe is not shown in joint practice, hence the stated reason.
- partner_embraer: consent assumed, as a CFM engine for a third airframer ('serve every airframer').
- open_fan and lobby_emissions: held, so no ask.
- genx: GE alone, no gate.
No Safran position is asserted [CX-0184].

DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD. These calls rest on doctrine:
- Embraer: no record; the NMA 'additive' rule [CX-0301] applied by inference.
- Lobby: profile §6.
- Supply load: Ali's seat doctrine, checked against the strain rule.
- The GEnx call: inference [CX-0599, CX-0615].

2035 REVIEW. If the bulletin shows no airframer launch and no rival engine, I reread the Ducted: a cancel then writes off $3.33B and saves $0.67B, and a reversal is in character. Ghai's numbers favour keeping it if an airframer launches in 2035. The Open Fan product call is made then, on Ali's test gates.

ExCo. Culp proposed and decided; Ghai and Ali concur on all five orders. No binding veto is triggered, so there are no overrides.

His binding vetoes do not touch this plan: the Open Fan, Lobby alone, GEnx beside a lone Ducted, a Ducted on an S1 expectation without weights, and price talk.

His record is thin. His own words end in March 2024 and cover engineering, at Medium confidence on durability, the test standard and RISE physics. On supply he states plainly that he has no evidence and follows doctrine [CX-0633]. I weighed his memo that way.
- Dates: taken in full. The ready years are the board's development times (Ducted 2036, Embraer counting 2037, GEnx 2042 or the first Re-engine, Open Fan 2045). Every row passes his binding date test.
- His candour that 2036 is a board rule, not a turn-on, turn-off result [CX-0009]: taken in full. That is why no Ducted, Embraer or GEnx date and no Open Fan entry year is in the public statement.

- Supply: his answer (no 'no', grid pays the strain, pace GEnx) agrees with doctrine. I checked it against the strain rule and adopted his pacing and supplier-watch condition as an operating move.
- RISE: his milestones for the 2035 product call are adopted as the gates.

board_guidance.expect_to_see:

(8) `premium_b` in dollars against the best plan in the expected column. Any RISE allowance must be stated separately in `premium_reason`; we expect none this round.
(9) Every override with its evidence.
(10) A public statement that names no rival, blames no one, gives no Open Fan entry before 2045, no untested Ducted date and no CFM price talk without Safran.
would_approve: `ducted: launch` if the expected column is one where an airframer launches (S2-S5). Item value against Do Nothing on its own: S2 +10.17, S3 +10.17, S4 +8.43, S5 +10.88. In Ducted + Embraer + GEnx, with Embraer defaulted alongside: +10.61, +13.05, +10.17, +12.85. All are above the $1B margin. The downside is bounded at its bill: S1 -4.00 against a $4B bill, or -6.00 against $6B with the strain; S6 -0.49 or -1.38. `partner_embraer: launch`, only with the Ducted launched this round and an expected column in S2-S5. recommendations.text: Safety first. Put Ali's readiness and durability review of any Ducted in the package, with test evidence behind the 2036 ready year. Have Culp strike or rebut his 20% fuel-burn red line in the rationale. We read a hard-rule-3 Ducted as a defence of the installed base; GE's next-generation engine stays RISE. No durability may be traded for fuel burn.

Delivery and timing. If you expect an airframer to launch this round, launch the Ducted now rather than in 2035. Launched now, it is ready in 2036, against an NGSA or a 7-year fps entering service in 2037 and a 10-year fps in 2040; a 2035 launch would not be ready until 2041. Say in the rationale why now rather than after the 2035 bulletin.

Put the expected column and weights for all six columns in `predictions`. Show each Board item against Do Nothing in the expected column and the worst column. On equal weights the Ducted package is worth +6.55 and the Ducted alone +5.86; tell us if your airframer reading differs.

Keep RISE funded as technology and bring the product decision to the 2035 round. A 2035 launch is still ready in 2045, and the bulletin will show by then whether any narrowbody can enter service earlier. If an airframer launches this round, say plainly that the Open Fan would wait and that 'ready by 2050' is out of reach on our tests, rather than stretching them. Keep the one RISE allowance unspent.

Cost and capital. Add a second or third project only where the grid pays the $2B strain: Embraer and GEnx together with the Ducted, never GEnx beside a lone Ducted. State every premium in dollars against the best plan in the expected column, with the RISE allowance shown separately. Keep the payout at no less than 70% of free cash flow; the package needs about $1.0B a year against about $2.5B of room. As real-world context, neither partner's analyst model carries a next engine, so tell us whether the Ducted would come out of buybacks and what Safran funds.

CFM parity rule. Name the Safran gate for each narrowbody order, with the reason Safran would agree. For a defensive Ducted, the reason is that it keeps both airframers on CFM. For Embraer, it is a CFM engine for a third airframer. The record shows no Safran position, so do not assert one.
Public statement: name no rival, blame no one, make no CFM price talk without Safran, give no Open Fan entry before 2045, and give no Ducted date that testing does not support.

frame.question: What game are we playing, and how do we win? [CX-0467] The game is the installed base on the next narrowbody, not share for its own sake. "Our major economics happen in and around the first and second" shop visit [CX-0422], and "we're not going for share" [CX-0493]. Nothing has launched, and "we don't have a birthright on that next order" [CX-0564]. Both new narrowbodies (fps and NGSA) are open this round, and orders are sealed and simultaneous, so any threat that lands this round has to be met this round. We win by doing three things. First, keep every new narrowbody on a CFM engine, with risk that is paid for. Second, keep the 787 on GEnx. Third, keep RISE whole as technology until an airframer wants it as a product [CX-0469, CX-0205]. So the question for this room is this. Do we launch a defensive Ducted now, ready in 2036 ahead of a 2037 entry, and do Partner Embraer and the GEnx upgrade ride with it under one strain charge? Or do we take GEnx alone and wait for the 2035 bulletin?
levers_in_play: ducted: hold | launch. A defensive lever under H3. $4B; ready at launch + 6, so 2036 if launched now. It adds +10 pp of NB share once a new NB is in service.
open_fan: hold | launch. $8B; ready at launch + 10 and not before 2045. Any 2030 airframe enters service in 2037-2040, so it would wait and take the 35 pp loss (20 pp with Lobby).
partner_embraer: hold | launch. It needs a new CFM engine launched. It counts 7 years after launch (2037) for +5 pp NB, and it counts as a project for strain.
lobby_emissions: hold | launch. $1B. It only caps the Open Fan loss at 20 pp and does nothing on its own.
genx: hold | upgrade_genx9 | invest_genx. The two are identical on the board: GE alone, +5 pp WB, counting from 2042 or from the first Re-engine's entry. Worth +0.77 to +0.78 alone in every column.
cancel: not in play. Nothing has launched yet. Strain of $2B applies once two or more projects run.
options_to_test: Row A, hold everything (Do Nothing, LEAP derivative; the reference row). By column S1-S6: 0.00 / -32.07 / -85.68 / -61.04 / -62.58 / -105.01.

Row B, GEnx upgrade alone. By column: +0.78 / -31.30 / -84.91 / -60.27 / -61.81 / -104.23. That is +0.77 to +0.78 against hold everywhere. GE alone. It is the best plan in S1 and S6, and the fallback if the Ducted fails a test.

Row C, Ducted alone. By column: -4.00 / -21.90 / -75.51 / -52.61 / -51.70 / -105.50. Against hold: -4.00, +10.17, +10.17, +8.43, +10.88, -0.49. S1 costs the whole $4B bill. In S2 it sits $1.21B below the best plan.

Row D, Ducted + Partner Embraer + GEnx upgrade (one $2B strain charge). By column: -5.22 / -20.69 / -71.86 / -50.10 / -48.96 / -105.61. Against GEnx alone: -6.00, +10.61, +13.05, +10.17, +12.85, -1.38. Against Ducted alone: -1.22, +1.21, +3.65, +2.51, +2.74, -0.11. It is the best grid plan in S2 to S5.

Row E, Ducted + Partner Embraer without GEnx. By column: -6.00 / -21.47 / -72.64 / -50.87 / -49.73 / -106.39. Tested to show that GEnx adds +0.77 to +0.78 inside the pair, because the pair already carries the strain.

Weighted check. On equal weights: Row D -50.41, C -51.87, B -56.96, A -57.73. On my preliminary weights (S1 .30, S2 .25, S3 .10, S4 .10, S5 .15, S6 .10): D -36.84, C -37.79, B -41.80, A -42.58. D's edge over C is only +0.95 there, inside the $1B ε, so the tie-break decides it. Both Ducted rows fall below GEnx alone once P(S1) passes about 0.60, with the rest spread evenly.

Timing check, which the grid cannot price. A Ducted launched now is ready in 2036; launched in 2035 it is ready in 2041. Ghai to size what waiting costs in the launch columns, and the salvage from a 2035 cancel (write-off of $4B x 5/6 = $3.33B).

Rows excluded unless a memo changes them, each recorded with its reason:
- Ducted + GEnx: -1.22 against Ducted alone in every column, from the strain.
- Open Fan: -8.00 to -57.60 against hold.
- Open Fan + Lobby: -11.00 to -40.76.
- Ducted + Open Fan: -14.00 to -51.20.
- Lobby alone: does nothing.
The Open Fan rows break H2, and the Board guidance would veto them.
red_lines: Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order [CX-0658]. No launch while a safety or durability flag from Ali stands unresolved by a cross-functional answer [CX-0012].
H1: never refuse an airframer and never lock one out. The LEAP derivative is an offer, and we want to be on all the critical platforms [CX-0587, CX-0185].

H2: never press an airframer into the Open Fan wait [CX-0205]. No Open Fan launch while a new NB can enter service before it is ready. Any airframe launched in 2030 enters service in 2037-2040, and the Open Fan is not ready before 2045. The one exception is the declared RISE allowance, and I do not plan to touch it this round.
H3: a Ducted only as a defence, never as the next-generation product [CX-0217, CX-0183]. The trigger has to be named: here it is the grid's slot-taking columns, S3 and S6.
H5: never cancel RISE for cost while an airframer may want it [CX-0174, CX-0398].
H6 (applied through Ali's test): no date without test evidence [CX-0009]. No untested Ducted date in public, and no Open Fan entry before 2045.
H7: the Safran gate on every CFM narrowbody order (Ducted, Open Fan, Embraer, Lobby) [CX-0184, CX-0166]. GEnx is GE alone.
H8: no public blame and no comment on rivals [CX-0625, CX-0580].
H9: doctrine plus objective premium at most $2.0B this round and $4.0B for the game. One RISE allowance of up to $15B, declared in full against the best non-RISE plan.

My line: a next engine needs at least a 20% fuel-burn improvement [CX-0217]. It binds RISE as the next generation. A defensive Ducted is not offered as the next generation (it gets 'less than half' the open fan's gain [CX-0183]), so the line does not bar it. I will rebut it in the rationale and never call the Ducted next-generation.
My line: durability is not traded for fuel burn [CX-0208].

This is a lean, not a decision; your memos decide it.

OPEN FAN: HOLD. RISE stays whole and funded as technology, with no cancel [CX-0214, CX-0174]. A 2030 launch is ready no sooner than a 2035 launch (both 2045) and waits in every launch column. The product call belongs to the 2035 round, the last one that can meet 'ready by 2050'. If an airframer launches now, we say plainly that the Open Fan would wait.

LOBBY: HOLD. It does nothing without an Open Fan.

DUCTED: LAUNCH NOW, AS A DEFENCE UNDER H3. The trigger is the grid's slot-taking columns, S3 (code 2) and S6 (codes 1 and 2), because no rival engine is on the record. It is worth +8.43 to +10.88 against hold wherever an airframer launches. Its loss is bounded at the $4B bill in S1 and is -0.49 in S6. Why now rather than after the 2035 bulletin: launched now it is ready in 2036, ahead of a 2037 entry; launched in 2035 it is ready only in 2041. The board charges R&D undiscounted, so waiting saves money only if no airframer ever launches.

EMBRAER AND GEnx: RIDE WITH THE DUCTED under one $2B strain charge, if two tests come back clean:
- Ghai's numbers keep the add-on more than $1B ahead of Ducted alone in my weights.
- Ali says the supply base carries three projects.
Inside ε, the tie-break is safety, quality, delivery and cost. So a supply 'no' from Ali drops Embraer, and GEnx goes too and waits for 2035.

FALLBACK: if the Ducted fails a test, GEnx alone, the best plan in S1 and S6.

EXPECTED COLUMN, PRELIMINARY: S2. Airbus launches NGSA and keeps today's dual-source A320neo pattern (code 6). I read that from the public pattern, not from a hoped-for selection. S2 sits below S1 for every plan, so it books PV low. Weights: S1 .30, S2 .25, S3 .10, S4 .10, S5 .15, S6 .10. The package is the best plan in S2, so the premium is nil; the RISE allowance stays unspent.

SAFRAN GATE:
- Ducted: consent assumed. The stated reason is that it keeps both airframers' next aircraft on CFM, and with them the aftermarket the partners split equally. A launch ahead of a committed airframe is not shown in joint practice, hence the stated reason.
- Embraer: consent assumed. It is a CFM engine for a third airframer, which fits 'serve every airframer'.
- GEnx: no gate; GE alone.
- Open Fan and Lobby: held, so no ask.

PUBLIC LINE: we serve every airframer; we tell you what we know and what we don't [CX-0436]; RISE remains our next generation; no date we have not tested; no rival named; no price talk. Keep the next narrowbody on CFM and pay only for the risk we can see. It's that simple, ain't that hard.

tests.threshold: Each launch's row beats hold in the expected column with its full bill charged: Ducted $4B, plus the $2B strain once two or more projects run. I use Culp's S2, which I accept, and check it on weights. Binding: capex (inference: the PV form of my price/cost rule).

Package (Ducted + Partner Embraer + GEnx upgrade): row -20.69, which is +11.38 against hold, +10.61 against GEnx alone (-31.30) and +1.21 against Ducted alone. Board items, each the submitted row minus the row with that item at hold (S2 / worst column): ducted, with Embraer defaulted alongside (package minus GEnx alone), +10.61 / S1 -6.00, equal to the $4B bill plus the $2B strain and not beyond it; partner_embraer (package minus Ducted + GEnx) +2.44 / S1 0.00; genx (package minus Ducted + Embraer) +0.78 / S4 and S5 +0.77. Weighted on Culp's weights (S1 .30, S2 .25, S3 .10, S4 .10, S5 .15, S6 .10): package -36.84, Ducted -37.79, GEnx -41.80, hold -42.58, so the package is +4.96 against GEnx alone. On my weights (S1 .35, S2 .20, S3 .10, S4 .10, S5 .15, S6 .10): package -36.07 against GEnx -40.20, or +4.13. On equal weights: +6.55. The package falls below GEnx alone once P(S1) passes about 0.60-0.62. Fails, so held: Open Fan against hold -8.00 to -57.60 (S2 -57.60); Open Fan + Lobby -11.00 to -40.76; Lobby alone costs $1B and does nothing; GEnx beside a lone Ducted is -1.22 to -1.23 in every column. Ask (1): your working numbers check out, all of them.

On the record (S1) the Ducted is -4.00 against hold and the package -6.00 against GEnx alone, so without the carve-out it fails. Hard rule 3 as mapped: S3 (NGSA, code 2) takes the Airbus slot. No volume or price number goes public.

tests.name: No overcapitalization (capex analogy to R&D)
tests.threshold: New R&D plus strain committed this round, spread over the development years, stays within about $2.5B a year. That is the cash left after returning more than 70% of about $8.5B of 2028 FCF; capex at 2-3% of revenue is the analogy. Binding: capex under the GM's rule (inference). It cannot fail on the board's numbers.
tests.numbers: Ducted $4B over 6 years is $0.67B a year, and the $2B strain over 6 is $0.33B a year. Embraer and GEnx carry no board R&D. Total $1.00B a year against $2.5B. Returning 70% of $8.5B ($5.95B) leaves about $1.5B to spare. Ask (4), Board guidance (labelled): yes, the 70% floor holds. Analyst context only, not the board: MS has GE returning about 94% of 2030E FCF ($13.5B), with buybacks of $10.0B (GS $7.0B) and gross debt flat. An unbudgeted $1.0B a year would therefore come out of buybacks, taking the payout to about 86%, still above 70%. GE's self-funded R&D in 2030E is $2.2-2.5B, so this is a real step-up, of the kind we already make for 'the future of flight'. Safran: neither partner's model carries a next engine. The Safran models show EUR 16-17B of net cash by 2030E. Joint practice on a 50/50 programme would share CFM spend, but no Safran position is on the record and I assert none. GEnx is GE alone.

cfo.would_change_mind_if:
Any one of these would change my recommendation:
- **Ali on supply.** He says the supply base can't carry three projects alongside the LEAP rate and the GE9X. Then Embraer and GEnx drop together and I recommend Ducted alone (-21.90 in S2).
- **Ali on durability or dates.** He raises a flag that isn't answered cross-functionally, or the 2036 ready year has no test behind it. Then GEnx alone (+0.78), and the Ducted waits for 2035.
- **Odds that nobody launches.** Confirmed data, not early signals, puts P(S1) above about 0.45-0.5, where waiting for the 2035 bulletin beats launching now, or above about 0.60, where GEnx alone beats the Ducted outright.
- **Safran.** It declines consent on the Ducted or Embraer.

What would strengthen the case:
- A rival NB engine is launched, committed or selected on the record, so hard rule 3 holds directly.
- An airframer commits volumes or a CFM selection. I'd book that upside then, not before.
- The GM's per-row share line shows the code-7 columns (S4, S5) below 50% without the Ducted, which strengthens the objective case.
cfo.memo:
Larry, I ran the money; there's nothing to hide. Each piece pays for itself in S2. The Ducted is +$10.17B against hold. The package is +$10.61B against GEnx alone and the best plan in S2 to S5, so the premium is nil. The downside stops at the bill: S1 costs $6.00B, the $4B plus the $2B strain, and no more. Weighted: +$4.96B on yours, +$4.13B on mine (more on S1). It stays ahead until the odds that nobody launches pass about 60%.

Volumes: nothing is agreed with either airframer, so on the record alone it fails. I accept hard rule 3 through S3, where a rival takes the Airbus slot: +$13.05B. S6 names the trigger but doesn't pay for it.

Capex: about $1.0B a year against $2.5B of room. The 70% payout stays whole.

Timing: waiting to 2035 costs about $4.3B in an NGSA-2037 column. Net of the S1 risk, launching now is worth $0.9-1.3B, and that edge goes once P(S1) passes about 0.45. It's closer than the grid makes it look.

Stack: the add-ons beat Ducted alone by $1.21B in S2 but by only $0.83-0.95B weighted, inside ε. That's Mohamed's supply call. If he says no, drop both. Never put GEnx beside a lone Ducted.

Open Fan and Lobby: hold. No price talk, and Safran on the Ducted and Embraer.

Guide: book no better than -$20.69B (I'd say -$21B) and raise when 2035 confirms. We've been proven wrong on dates before.

tests.name: Turn on, turn off (my veto: dates)
tests.threshold: No ready year earlier than the board's development time: Ducted launch + 6; Open Fan launch + 10 and not before 2045; Embraer counts 7 years after launch; GEnx 3 years after launch, not before 2035 (the first possible Re-engine entry) and 2042 if no Re-engine. An order whose value depends on an earlier date fails (inference: my test standard applied to the board's development times).
tests.numbers: Ducted: launch 2030, ready 2036 (2030 + 6, not earlier). Launched in 2035 instead: ready 2041, so Culp's timing check is right. Open Fan (held): launch 2030 gives 2040, floored to 2045; launch 2035 gives 2045. The same year either way. Partner Embraer: launch 2030, counts 2037. It rides on the Ducted, which is ready in 2036, so the count year is after the engine's ready year. GEnx upgrade: launch 2030 + 3 = 2033, held back to the first Re-engine entry (2035 at the earliest, for a 2030 Re-engine) or to 2042 if neither airframer re-engines. Culp's 'from 2042 or the first Re-engine's entry' is correct. Every row in the frame passes: A hold, B GEnx, C Ducted, D Ducted + Embraer + GEnx, E Ducted + Embraer. No row's value rests on a year earlier than launch plus development time.

tests.name: Test, not analysis (my veto: dates)
tests.threshold: Every date in the public statement or other moves must be one a test can back: no Open Fan entry before 2045, and no ready date before launch plus development years. A Ducted date that no test backs stays out of the statement.
tests.numbers: Answer to Culp's ask 1: 2036 is the board's development time (launch + 6), not a test result. No Ducted engine has been turned on and turned off. RISE technology has test history in Culp's words: over 350 programme tests with an early focus on durability [CX-0216], and HPT-blade dust testing on the compact core [CX-0222]. Those tests are RISE technology, not this engine. The 2036 date is valid inside the ExCo and for the Board's arithmetic. It is not a public date. Culp's draft public line ('no date we have not tested', 'RISE remains our next generation') carries no date, so this passes now. It stays a pass only if the step-4 statement gives no Ducted ready year, no Embraer or GEnx date and no Open Fan entry before 2045.

tests.name: Ready no later than the airframe: Ducted (advice)
tests.threshold: Report the gap in years between the Ducted ready year and the first new narrowbody's entry. A defensive Ducted earns +10 pp from its ready year once a new NB is in service. Earlier is better, but a late date does not fail it. Not a veto ground (inference).
tests.numbers: Ducted ready 2036. Against NGSA launched 2030 (entry 2037; S2, S3, S5, S6) or a 7-year fps (entry 2037): 1 year ahead. Against a 10-year fps or the Embraer route (entry 2040; S4): 4 years ahead. S1: no airframe, so no gap. Nothing we rely on rests on a year before 2036. If the Ducted waits for the 2035 round: ready 2041, 4 years late against a 2037 entry and 1 year late against 2040, and the +10 pp counts only from 2041. Grid, Ducted against hold: S1 -4.00, S2 +10.17, S3 +10.17, S4 +8.43, S5 +10.88, S6 -0.49.

tests.name: Ready no later than the airframe: Open Fan (advice)
tests.threshold: The Open Fan must be ready no later than the first new narrowbody's entry, or the board takes 35 pp of NB share (20 pp with Lobby). Report the gap. Not a veto ground, because the 2045 ready year itself is correct (inference).
tests.numbers: Answer to Culp's ask 2: the Open Fan is ready in 2045 whether launched in 2030 (2040, floored to 2045) or in 2035. Against a 2037 entry (NGSA, or a 7-year fps launched 2030) it is 8 years late. Against a 2040 entry (10-year fps, Embraer route) it is 5 years late. It would be late against any airframe launched this round, so H2 binds. Grid: Open Fan rows -8.00 (S1) to -57.60 against hold, and Open Fan + Lobby -11.00 to -40.76. This fails for any Open Fan launch this round. Culp holds it, so no order fails.

tests.name: Physics
tests.threshold: Call RISE the next generation only at 20% or better. A ducted engine has 'less than half' the open fan's gain, so it is never the next generation. That it is a defensive step only is company doctrine (hard rule 3), not my words. The brief has no fuel-burn data, so this is a wording check on the public line (inference).
tests.numbers: Answer to Culp's ask 4: confirmed, in my own words. RISE gives 'more than 20%' [CX-0001]; 20% is 'practically impossible ... without the open fan. And the reason is physics' [CX-0180]; a ducted engine 'has less than half the fuel burn improvements that can come from an open fan' [CX-0183]. A Ducted cannot meet Culp's 20% line, so it can stand only as a defence under H3, with the trigger in the grid's slot-taking columns S3 and S6. Culp's draft public line keeps RISE as the next generation and does not call the Ducted that: pass. It fails at step 4 if the statement calls the Ducted next-generation or makes a fuel-burn claim for it.

tests.name: Durability first
tests.threshold: No plan trades durability or time on wing for fuel burn or schedule. The brief has no durability data, so this is not applicable unless the brief or a statement makes a durability claim (inference; Culp's line applied to my seat).
tests.numbers: Answer to Culp's ask 3: I raise no safety or durability flag on the Ducted, Embraer or GEnx. The brief carries no durability data, and no order or draft line trades durability for fuel burn or makes a durability claim. That is not a clearance of the engine. It means the durability gates come later, at design and test reviews, against the turn-on, turn-off standard. Any time-on-wing claim in the statement would need test or field data, as the LEAP numbers did (9,882 cycles against about 17,000 for the CFM56) [CX-0006].

tests.name: Supply load (seat doctrine)
tests.threshold: Two or more projects cost $2B of strain and load the same constrained suppliers: recommend against stacking unless the grid pays more than the strain (inference; my supply role is in Culp's words only).
tests.numbers: Answer to Culp's ask 5. No evidence in my record on supply rates: following doctrine (the strain rule). Package D against Ducted alone C, by column: S1 -1.22, S2 +1.21, S3 +3.65, S4 +2.51, S5 +2.74, S6 -0.11. Gross Embraer + GEnx before the strain: +0.78, +3.21, +5.65, +4.51, +4.74, +1.89, against $2B. Weighted net: +0.95 on Culp's weights (D -36.84 against C -37.79) and +1.46 on equal weights (D -50.41 against C -51.87). The grid pays the strain in S2-S5 and on both weightings. On Culp's weights the margin is inside the $1B epsilon. I have no test or field data that the base cannot carry three projects on top of the LEAP rate, the GE9X ramp and the durability kits, and none that it can. So I give no supply 'no'. Condition (inference): pace the GEnx upgrade work behind the Ducted's peak, since GEnx counts no earlier than 2035 and 2042 without a Re-engine, and watch the 9 suppliers at 15 sites that caused 80% of shortages [CX-0613]. Ducted + GEnx without Embraer fails this test: -1.22 to -1.23 in every column.

tests.name: Fix, don't redesign
tests.threshold: On the widebody, prefer the GEnx upgrade on a proven architecture over a new engine. On the narrowbody, keep RISE technology flowing into LEAP upgrades while RISE matures. This does not argue against the Open Fan as the next generation (inference).
tests.numbers: Answer to Culp's ask 6, GEnx: upgrade_genx9 is a derivative on the GE90/GEnx architecture and is preferred. On the board it equals invest_genx: +0.77 to +0.78 in every column. Any GEnx date we state needs test support like any other, so state none. Its count year is 2042, or the first Re-engine's entry (2035 at the earliest). LEAP: the Do Nothing derivative keeps taking RISE technology. The Ducted does not replace RISE, and RISE stays whole as technology.

tests.name: Safety call
tests.threshold: If a problem in the brief or an order touches safety or durability, it needs a cross-functional team, not one person.
tests.numbers: No problem in the brief touches safety. No order this round carries a safety finding. Every Ducted design and test gate from here will be a cross-functional call: 'No single person can make a safety decision.' This is standing practice, not a flag.

tests.numbers: Launch 2030, counts 2037. It rides on the Ducted, ready 2036. No engineering evidence on Embraer in my record: following Culp and doctrine. State no Embraer date in public.

tests.threshold: Before the 2035 product call (launch 2035, ready 2045, the last launch that meets 'ready by 2050'), RISE must be turned on and turned off in test, not in analysis (inference: my standard applied to the product call).
tests.numbers: There is no Open Fan order this round. The milestones I would want in hand by 2035 (inference): (1) the ground and flight test, which slipped from 'by the middle of this decade' [CX-0151] to 'this decade' [CX-0211], done and reported back against that promise; (2) compact-core durability turned on and off, with HPT dust testing [CX-0222] closed and the open-fan durability owner [CX-0223] showing no open failure; (3) more than 20% fuel burn shown in engine test, not analysis [CX-0001, CX-0008]; (4) engine-level noise below today's LEAP, with Airbus [CX-0013]. Without them, a 2045 ready year is a board rule, not a promise. Promise no RISE date.

vetoes.plan: open_fan: launch this round, alone or in any combination (the Open Fan rows, and Ducted + Open Fan)
vetoes.ground: Advice only, not a date veto. Ready no later than the airframe: the Open Fan is ready in 2045, whether launched in 2030 or 2035. That is 8 years after a 2037 NGSA or 7-year fps entry and 5 years after a 2040 entry, so the board takes 35 pp of NB share (20 pp with Lobby): -8.00 to -57.60 against hold. The 2045 ready year itself is correct, so my binding date ground does not apply. No RISE flight-test result is in hand to back any earlier promise.

vetoes.plan: Ducted + GEnx upgrade without Partner Embraer
vetoes.ground: Advice only (supply load, seat doctrine). It triggers the $2B strain for one small project: -1.22 to -1.23 against Ducted alone in every column. The grid does not pay the strain.

vetoes.plan: Pre-notice, not an objection to the orders: a public statement or other move that states a Ducted ready or entry year (2036 or any other), an Embraer or GEnx date, an Open Fan entry before 2045, or a fuel-burn or durability claim for the Ducted
vetoes.ground: Binding ground 2 (dates not backed by real testing): 2036 is the board's development time (launch + 6), not a turn-on, turn-off result, and no Ducted engine has been tested. No statement exists yet, so nothing is vetoed now. If the step-4 statement carries such a date, I veto it then, and it binds unless Culp answers it with test evidence. Note: my veto right over programme dates is an inference. My words date from 2024, as VP of Engineering, and concern believing durability-fix results; the team rule and the GM read them as a binding date test.

ops.would_change_mind_if: Only test or field data, not analysis. (1) A Ducted or core test, or a RISE-component test the Ducted would draw on, showing a failure not yet turned off, or a slip that puts the 2036 ready year at risk. I would then flag durability and the date, and the Ducted waits for a cross-functional answer. (2) Supplier field data: shortages concentrating again in the few suppliers and sites behind 80% of the 2024 shortages, LEAP or GE9X deliveries missing on the same suppliers, or a supply-chain crunch. I would then give a supply 'no': drop Embraer, with GEnx going with it, and keep the Ducted alone. (3) A durability finding in the brief, such as an engine maturity slip. That would bring a durability flag. (4) For the 2035 product call: RISE flight test done, core durability turned on and off, and more than 20% fuel burn shown in engine test, with no new narrowbody able to enter service before 2045. I would then back an Open Fan launch with a 2045 ready year, and still promise no earlier date. (5) A Re-engine on the public record would move the GEnx count year to that Re-engine's entry, 2035 at the earliest. I would recheck that date, not the order.
ops.memo:
Larry, testing, not analysis.

Dates. Every row passes. Ducted: 2030 plus 6 is 2036, one year ahead of an NGSA or 7-year fps in 2037, four ahead of a 2040 fps. Embraer counts 2037, after the engine it rides on. GEnx counts 2042, or from the first Re-engine, never before 2035. Open Fan: 2045 launched in 2030 or 2035, eight years late against 2037. H2 binds. Hold it.

But 2036 is the board's development time, not a test. No Ducted engine has been turned on and turned off; RISE tests are not this engine. So 2036 stays in this room. No Ducted, Embraer or GEnx date, and no Open Fan entry before 2045, in the statement, or I veto it at step 4.

Physics. A ducted engine has less than half the open fan's gain. The reason is physics. It cannot meet your 20% line: a defence, never the next generation.

Durability and safety. No durability data in the brief; no order trades durability for fuel burn. I raise no flag. That is not a clearance: every design gate is a cross-functional call.

Supply. No evidence: following doctrine. The grid pays the $2B strain: the package beats Ducted alone by 0.95 on your weights, 1.46 on equal. No supply 'no'; pace GEnx behind the Ducted.

Embraer, Lobby: no evidence, following Culp.

RISE by 2035: flight test done, core durability turned on and off, 20% shown in test.

Launch Ducted, Embraer, GEnx upgrade. Hold Open Fan, Lobby.

other_moves.move: Offer a CFM engine to every airframer on every new narrowbody
other_moves.detail: This is H1: we refuse no airframer and lock none out [CX-0587, CX-0185]. The offer is a LEAP derivative or the new ducted engine, as each customer chooses. No price or terms are stated in public: CFM narrowbody pricing is a joint decision with Safran [CX-0184].

other_moves.move: CFM partner consultation on the Ducted and Embraer launches
other_moves.detail: Both CFM orders go through CFM governance with Safran. Consent is assumed, with stated reasons. The Ducted keeps both airframers' next aircraft on a CFM engine, and with them the aftermarket the partners split equally. Embraer puts a CFM engine in front of a third airframer, which fits 'serve every airframer'. The record shows no Safran position, so none is asserted. GEnx is GE alone and needs no gate.

other_moves.move: Supply-base readiness for a three-project stack (FLIGHT DECK reviews)
other_moves.detail: Ali's condition is taken up. GEnx upgrade work is paced behind the Ducted's development peak; GEnx counts no earlier than 2042 without a Re-engine. Monthly operating reviews cover the 9 suppliers at 15 sites behind 80% of past shortages [CX-0613]. LEAP OE delivery and spares come first, and spares never crowd out OE [CX-0529]. The trigger to drop Embraer and GEnx is a supply 'no' from Ali on field data.

other_moves.move: Cross-functional design and test gates on the Ducted
other_moves.detail: Every Ducted design and test gate is a cross-functional call, never one person's [CX-0012]. Durability is not traded for fuel burn or schedule [CX-0208]. The 2036 ready year stays inside the company until a turn-on, turn-off test backs it [CX-0009].

other_moves.move: Keep RISE funded as technology and set the gates for the 2035 product call
other_moves.detail: There is no cancel and no 'program dividend' [CX-0174, CX-0214]. Ali's milestones must be in hand by the 2035 round: (1) the ground and flight test done; (2) compact-core durability turned on and off, with the HPT dust testing closed; (3) more than 20% fuel burn shown in engine test, not analysis; (4) noise below today's LEAP. The product call is made in 2035, on the bulletin and these tests.

other_moves.move: Fund the package inside the capital allocation framework
other_moves.detail: The package needs about $1.0B a year of new R&D and strain ($0.67B Ducted plus $0.33B strain) against about $2.5B of room. Returns stay at or above 70% of FCF [CX-0645], and the A-range balance sheet is held. Any unbudgeted spend comes out of buybacks, not the dividend or the rating. That is analyst context only, per Ghai.

decision.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That doesn't change this year.

Let me tell you what we know and what we don't. Nothing new has launched yet in the narrowbody. When it does, our customers decide the aircraft and the timing, not us, and we don't have a birthright on that next order. So CFM is launching a new ducted engine programme, so that every airframer has a CFM engine to choose on whatever comes next. CFM is also partnering with Embraer, putting a CFM engine in front of a third airframer. And at GE we're launching a GEnx upgrade for the 787 and the airlines that fly it.

RISE remains our next generation. We're all in on the open fan technology, and it stays funded. But it's really not for us to say when that architecture enters service. If an airframer launches a new narrowbody now, the open fan won't be ready for it, and we won't ask anyone to wait.

Here's what we don't know: which aircraft launch, when, and with which engines. We won't give you dates our testing hasn't earned. You'll get them when it has. We'll fund this within our capital allocation framework and keep the balance sheet where it is. We want to be on all the critical platforms that matter in the decades ahead. It's that simple, ain't that hard.
decision.rationale:
DECISION. Launch the Ducted, Partner Embraer and the GEnx upgrade (upgrade_genx9). Hold the Open Fan and Lobby. Nothing is cancelled. All five orders follow the frame, and both memos recommend the same five.

WHAT GAME, HOW WE WIN [CX-0467]. The game is the installed base on the next narrowbody [CX-0422], not share for its own sake [CX-0493]. Both new narrowbodies, fps and NGSA, are open, and orders are sealed. Hold loses -32.07 to -105.01 in every column where an airframer launches. S3 (NGSA, code 2) and S6 (codes 1 and 2) are the columns where a rival selection takes CFM's slot. "We don't have a birthright on that next order" [CX-0564].

TESTS
(1) Additive and paid for the risk [CX-0301]. The package, Ducted + Partner Embraer + GEnx upgrade, is the best grid plan in S2 to S5: S2 -20.69, S3 -71.86, S4 -50.10, S5 -48.96. Its S1 cost is named: -5.22 against hold, or -6.00 against GEnx alone, which is the $4B bill plus the $2B strain and no more. The risk is worth it because the package is worth +10.61 to +13.05 wherever an airframer launches, and the loss is capped at the bill when none does.

(2) Low case first [CX-0248, CX-0536]. The expected column is S2: Airbus launches NGSA and keeps today's dual-source A320neo pattern (code 6). That is the record's pattern, not a hoped-for selection. S2 sits below S1 for every plan, so it books low.

(3) Hard rule 3. The trigger is the grid's slot-taking columns, because no rival engine is launched, committed or selected on the record. S3 is the column that pays it: the Ducted is worth +10.17 against hold, and the package +13.05 against GEnx alone. S6 names the trigger but does not pay it (-0.49, or -1.38). Ghai accepts the trigger through S3, not S6.

(4) My 20% line, rebutted. The 20% line [CX-0217] binds the next-generation product, which is RISE. The ducted engine has "less than half the fuel burn improvements" of an open fan [CX-0183; Ali, CX-0180]. It cannot meet 20%, and it is not offered as the next generation. It is a defence of the installed base under hard rule 3, and it is never called next-generation in public. The durability line [CX-0208] stands: Ali raises no durability or safety flag, and every design gate is cross-functional [CX-0012].

(5) Supply. Two or more projects draw the $2B strain. The grid pays it in S2 to S5. Ali gives no supply 'no', on condition that GEnx is paced behind the Ducted's peak.

WHY NOW, NOT AFTER THE 2035 BULLETIN. Launched now, the Ducted is ready in 2036 against a 2037 entry (NGSA or a 7-year fps) and a 2040 entry (10-year fps or the Embraer route). Launched in 2035, it is ready only in 2041. Ghai sizes the cost of waiting at about $4.3B in S2 and S3, $4.5B in S5 and $1.1B in S4. Waiting saves $0.49B in S6, and in S1 it saves up to $4.00B. Net edge for launching now: +$1.06B to +$1.26B on my weights, +$0.64B to +$0.88B on his. Waiting wins only once P(S1) passes about 0.45. Ghai's numbers show deferring Embraer or GEnx to 2035 would still draw the strain while the Ducted is in development, so it saves nothing.

THE STACK, AND MY OWN CONDITION MISSED. I said the add-ons had to clear Ducted alone by more than $1B on my weights. They clear it by $0.95B, missing by $0.05B: inside ε. Elsewhere they clear it by +$1.21B in S2, +$1.46B on equal weights and +$0.83B on Ghai's. They lose $1.22B in S1 and $0.11B in S6. So the tie-break decides, "safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order" [CX-0658]:
- Safety: a tie. No flag on either plan.
- Quality: a tie on the evidence. The grid charges the load at $2B, and Ali has no test or field data either way. I don't invent a flag. I take his pacing condition and the supplier watch.
- Delivery: the package wins. It puts a CFM engine in front of a third airframer and keeps the 787 on product (H1: "on all the critical platforms" [CX-0587]).
It is decided at delivery, with cost (+$0.95B weighted, best plan in S2) confirming it. GEnx never sits beside a lone Ducted (-1.22 to -1.23 in every column).

HELD
- Open Fan: launched now it is ready in 2045, the same as a 2035 launch. It waits in every launch column, at -$8.00B to -$57.60B against hold (H2) [CX-0205]. RISE stays whole as technology (H5) [CX-0174, CX-0214].
- Lobby: does nothing without an Open Fan.

BOARD ITEMS, BY COLUMN, S1 / S2 / S3 / S4 / S5 / S6
- Submitted package: -5.22 / -20.69 / -71.86 / -50.10 / -48.96 / -105.61. Against Do Nothing in S2 that is +11.38; the worst column against Do Nothing is S1, at -5.22.
- ducted (package minus GEnx alone, Embraer defaulted with it): -6.00 / +10.61 / +13.05 / +10.17 / +12.85 / -1.38. Weighted +4.96. The worst is S1 at -6.00, equal to its $6B bill.
- partner_embraer (package minus Ducted + GEnx): 0.00 / +2.44 / +4.88 / +3.73 / +3.97 / +1.12. Weighted +2.18. It never goes below zero.
- genx (package minus Ducted + Embraer): +0.78 / +0.78 / +0.78 / +0.77 / +0.77 / +0.78.

SAFRAN GATE (H7, CFM parity rule)
- ducted: consent assumed, because it keeps both airframers' next aircraft on CFM and the aftermarket the partners split equally. A launch ahead of a committed airframe is not shown in joint practice, hence the stated reason.
- partner_embraer: consent assumed, as a CFM engine for a third airframer ('serve every airframer').
- open_fan and lobby_emissions: held, so no ask.
- genx: GE alone, no gate.
No Safran position is asserted [CX-0184].

DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD. These calls rest on doctrine:
- Embraer: no record; the NMA 'additive' rule [CX-0301] applied by inference.
- Lobby: profile §6.
- Supply load: Ali's seat doctrine, checked against the strain rule.
- The GEnx call: inference [CX-0599, CX-0615].

2035 REVIEW. If the bulletin shows no airframer launch and no rival engine, I reread the Ducted: a cancel then writes off $3.33B and saves $0.67B, and a reversal is in character. Ghai's numbers favour keeping it if an airframer launches in 2035. The Open Fan product call is made then, on Ali's test gates.

ExCo. Culp proposed and decided; Ghai and Ali concur on all five orders. No binding veto is triggered, so there are no overrides.

Statement. I read it line by line. It gives no Ducted, Embraer or GEnx year and no Open Fan entry year; 'this year' is the only year in it. H3, for the Board. The defensive trigger is anticipatory. It rests on the grid's slot-taking columns (S3, S6), because no rival engine is on the record yet. recommendations.text:
Safety and quality. We read Ali's 'no flag' as he wrote it: it is not a clearance.
- Bring each Ducted design and test gate to the full board as it occurs. Each one is a cross-functional call.
- Put turn-on, turn-off evidence behind the 2036 ready year before any Ducted date goes public. Durability is not traded for fuel burn or schedule.
- Bring us at once any slip beyond the one year of float to 2037. Ghai puts it at about $1.0-1.2B a year in S2.

Quality and supply.
- Keep Ali's conditions in the monthly reviews: GEnx paced behind the Ducted's peak, and the watch on the 9 suppliers at 15 sites.
- If a supply 'no' or a later cancel drops Embraer, retest GEnx net of the strain it would then add. Beside a lone Ducted it is -1.22 to -1.23 in every column. Bring the two to us together.

Delivery, for the 2035 round.
- Reread the Ducted on our cancellation test. A cancel passes only if it is worth at least zero in every plausible column.
- A cancel of an engine an airframe has selected also needs a stated reason why Safran would agree.
- Show the $3.33B write-off beside the cost of keeping the programme.
- Bring the RISE product decision to that round on Ali's milestones: flight test done, compact-core durability turned on and off, and more than 20% fuel burn shown in engine test. It becomes a product only on an airframer path.
- Keep the one RISE allowance unspent, and declare it separately if it is ever used.

CFM parity rule (Safran consent).
- The public statement announces two CFM launches with consent assumed, not given.
- Record Safran's actual answer from CFM governance in the 2035 notes, together with what Safran funds. If it declines, withdraw plainly, as Ghai says.
- From now on, present CFM programmes in public as joint with our partner.
- Assert no Safran position until one is on the record.

Cost and capital. The case is thinner than the grid's $10B suggests.
- The Ducted item stays ahead of GEnx alone only while the chance that no airframer launches (S1) is below about 0.62.
- Launching now beats waiting for 2035 only below about 0.45 (Ghai), worth $0.6-1.3B net.
- Carry that chance and all six column weights in each round's predictions.
- Keep booking low; -21.0 is right.
- Keep the 70% payout whole, with the package at about $1.0B a year.
- Keep the premium count: $0 of $2.0B this round, $0 of $4.0B for the game, and the RISE allowance $0 of $15B.

Objective. Say plainly in the notes that NB share stays below 50% in S3 and S6 even with the package: about 43% in S3 in 2040, on Ghai's arithmetic. We spend no premium on that leg unless the grid pays for it.

The Ducted is ready in 2036, ahead of a 2037 entry. Ali raises no flag, Ghai and Ali concur, and no veto stands. Culp's 20% line is rebutted. pratt_whitney.public_statement:
Bad news first. For too long the GTF fleet was not where it needed to be, and we own that. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF, and the fleet comes first. We keep inserting the Hot Section durability kit across the fleet, and no new programme takes parts or engineers away from that work. We control what we can control.

Pratt & Whitney will commit its next-generation geared turbofan, GTF2, in any round an airframer selects it, sole source or shared, on standard commercial terms. GTF2 will be ready six years from launch: 2036 for a 2030 commitment, and no earlier. Every life-limited part will be at full life at entry into service, and durability will be validated in severe-environment testing before then. If anything has to give, the date moves, not the testing.

We are making no Joint Venture commitment this round. We will not speak for any airframer's plans, dates or rates; those are theirs to announce. These are responsible bets with responsible paybacks.
pratt_whitney.rationale:
DECISION: `gtf2_solo: launch_if_selected`, `jv_with_rr: hold`. Eddy proposed it, Mitchill recommends it, and the Board approves it at any weights. Overrides: none.

1. CONSTRAINT FIRST: safety and durability [PX-0035][PX-0073]
- Eddy's readiness check binds me, and it passes. GTF2 launched in 2030 is ready in 2036:
  - NGSA EIS 2037: 1 year of margin;
  - fps 7-year EIS 2037: 1 year;
  - fps 10-year or via Embraer EIS 2040: 4 years.
- A 2035 trigger would be ready in 2041, too late for any 2030 airframe. Only a 2030 order can answer a 2030 selection.
- One year of margin is thin. Eddy's own certification slipped from mid-2024 to 2025, and my operating dates have slipped by between one quarter and two years [PX-0017][PX-0098][PX-0104]. So I discount my own dates and take his condition: the durability programme stays intact, and if anything gives, the date moves, not the testing.
- Parts: the bulletin shows no live fleet, quality or supply problem. As Eddy says, this passes on the board, not on data. GTF2 test hardware and the ramp are ring-fenced away from the AOG recovery and kit insertion. The fleet beats a new engine [PX-0080].

2. BINDING VETOES, all respected
- Mitchill, ground 4, binding: no `jv_with_rr: commit`. Rolls-Royce is not on the record and no live airframe carries an RR code. I hold the Joint Venture.
- Mitchill's conditional ground-2 veto on `launch` is not invoked at his weights (+$0.34B edge with the corrected cancel). It does not bite, because I do not submit `launch`.
- Eddy: no binding veto. Both his grounds pass for `launch_if_selected`.
- The `overrides` field is empty.

3. THE GRID, rows S1-S7 ($B)
- `launch_if_selected`: 0 / +22.73 / -27.76 / +19.31 / +22.00 / -27.76 / 0.
- Do Nothing (`hold`): 0 / -27.76 / -27.76 / -2.85 / -27.76 / -27.76 / 0.
- Board item, `launch_if_selected` minus `hold`: 0 / +50.49 / 0 / +22.16 / +49.76 / 0 / 0. It is never negative.
- `launch` minus `launch_if_selected`: -2.00 / 0 / +3.79 / 0 / 0 / +3.79 / -2.00.

4. EXPECTED VALUES
- My weights: S1 0.28 / S2 0.22 / S3 0.17 / S4 0.05 / S5 0.08 / S6 0.10 / S7 0.10. I blended my frame prior toward Mitchill's timing read.

| Plan | My weights | Mitchill's weights |
|---|---:|---:|
| `launch_if_selected` + `hold` | +0.23 | -1.72 |
| `launch` + `hold` | +0.49 | -1.38 |
| Do Nothing | -15.97 | -15.41 |
| `launch_if_selected` + commit | +0.03 | |

- `launch_if_selected` against `hold`: +$16.20B at my weights, +$13.69B at Mitchill's.

5. THE HEDGE TEST
- Edge of `launch` over `launch_if_selected` = 3.79 × (pS3 + pS6) − 2.00 × (pS1 + pS7):

| Weights | Edge ($B) |
|---|---:|
| Mine | +0.26 |
| Mitchill's | +0.34 |
| My frame prior | +0.25 |
| Equal | +0.51 |

- At my weights and at Mitchill's, the edge is positive, so it clears Mitchill's ground 2. It is below the Board's +$0.5B franchise-defence bar, which only equal weights reach, just barely. Even crediting a 2035 cancel in S1 and S7, it reaches only +$0.39B (mine) and +$0.47B (Mitchill's). The Board wants the launch to stand without the option.
- Its case rests on S3 and S6 alone. S2, S4 and S5 are identical for both orders.
- The Board would veto `launch`, and I have no override against the Board. So `launch_if_selected` is both the doctrine order and the best plan that passes.

6. RESPONSIBLE BET: premium declared [PX-0010]
- Doctrine premium: $0.26B at my weights ($0.34B at Mitchill's). That is the PV I give up against the unconditional `launch` to keep the 'no new engine without a committed airframer' rule [P-0746][PX-0109][PX-0009].
- Objective premium: $0, explained in section 7.
- Total: $0.26B, inside the $1B cap.
- No Board item trails `hold`, so no Board premium is needed.

7. OBJECTIVE
- `launch_if_selected` and `launch` meet Restore credibility in the same columns: S2, S4 and S5 (p = 0.35).
- `launch_if_selected` meets Capitalise (ΔPV ≥ 0) in S1, S2, S4, S5 and S7 (p = 0.73). `launch` meets it only in S2, S4 and S5, because S1 and S7 come in at -2.00.
- So the objective does not favour `launch` on the grid. The off-grid chance of answering a 2035 NGSA switch to a P&W code is not booked (Mitchill's ground 4, confirmed).

8. MISS-A-CYCLE TEST [PX-0071][P-1347]
- Losing our half of the A320neo slot costs -27.76. `launch_if_selected` answers any 2030 selection in time.
- 'Miss a cycle' beats 'cross that bridge' only on visible demand. `launch_if_selected` makes the spend coincide with that demand.
- 'Miss a cycle' was said of RTX's businesses in general; applying it to GTF2 is inference.

9. SHARED-SOURCE DOCTRINE RELIEF, declared
- `launch_if_selected` fires on codes 6 and 7 as well as 2. Every selection column on this grid is shared: S2 (code 6), S4 (code 7), S5 (codes 7 and 6).
- I accept shared source against the sole-source rule [P-0746] as declared doctrine relief. The company accepts 40-50% of a shared platform [P-1292], and we aimed for about 40% of the A320neo [PX-0058].
- On NGSA it is also franchise defence (inference).

10. CANCEL TEST
- I adopt Mitchill's correction. For a triggered GTF2 that later loses its code: cancel in 2035 only if no live new narrowbody carries a P&W code, and only if the 2035 hold row does not beat the cancel row. The write-off is $1.67B and the cancel saves $0.33B.
- I reject the literal test 'cancel if no selection'.

11. DIVIDEND AND DEBT [PX-0081][P-0669][P-0686]
- Nothing is spent unless an airframer selects us. Then the cost is about $0.33B a year from 2030 to 2035, about 5.6% of the ~$6B envelope.
- On the analyst baseline, this competes with buybacks only. The dividend is covered, net debt is below 1x EBITDA by 2030E, and no envelope stretch is needed.

12. VALUE, NOT SHARE
- Standard terms. The Hot Section kit is charged. No concession in other moves or in the statement [PX-0055][PX-0100].

13. JOINT VENTURE
- `hold`. Revisit in 2035 on the trigger written into other moves.
- I have no record of my own here, so the view is doctrine plus Mitchill's and Eddy's tests.

14. BIASES, displayed
- Optimism on dates: I state no EIS, and I give no ready year before launch + 6.
- Incrementalism: I assumed the next single-aisle 'mid-next decade' [PX-0093]. Its failure mode, missing a round-1 selection, is closed by `launch_if_selected`.
- Supply-first caution: this is partly why I keep `launch_if_selected` over `launch`. Its cost is declared as the $0.26B premium.
- Architecture loyalty: GTF2 first, Joint Venture on hold. That is consistent with the unmet conditions, but flagged.

15. THIN RECORD
- I have made no launch decision, so my launch thresholds are inference (Medium).
- 'Miss a cycle' and 'demand visibility' are RTX-wide statements.
- My Joint Venture view is Low and rests on doctrine.

- I take his wording advice in the public statement: full-life LLPs at entry into service and severe-environment validation, not field time on wing.
- His parts pass is on the board, not on data, and I record it that way.
- He proposes no unconditional `launch` except into a P&W code on the record. That matches the Board.

frame.question: Control what you can control. Nobody has launched anything yet, but 2030 is the round in which a new NGSA or fps would choose its engines. GTF2 launched this round is ready in 2036, so it is the only P&W engine that can meet a 2030 airframe's entry into service (NGSA 2037; fps 2037 on the 7-year route, 2040 on the 10-year or Embraer route). A trigger in 2035 would be ready in 2041, too late for a 2030 NGSA. So the question this round is which order puts GTF2 on any 2030 airframe that selects us without spending $2B on an engine nobody has asked for. The second question: is an unselected NGSA franchise hedge (`launch`) worth losing $2.00B in S1 and S7 to gain $3.79B in S3 and S6? The fleet comes first throughout. Is the demand visible, do the business model, timing and volume work, and is durability mature at entry into service?

  - edge below 0: B is struck on his ground 2;
  - edge between 0 and +$0.5B: the Board would veto B, so I keep `launch_if_selected` and declare a doctrine premium equal to the edge (within the $1B cap);
  - edge of +$0.5B or more, with Eddy's readiness and parts pass: I would weigh B as NGSA franchise defence, with the 2035 cancel ($1.67B) written in.

Joint Venture: `hold`. Revisit in 2035 if Rolls-Royce commits publicly or an airframe carries code 1, 4, 5 or 7, with the gear and core technology protected.

Other moves (public, no effect on the board): GTF Hot Section durability kit insertion continues across the fleet on standard commercial terms.

PROPOSED DISCLOSURE: "We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF, and the fleet comes first. Pratt & Whitney will commit its next-generation geared turbofan, GTF2, in any round an airframer selects it, sole or shared source, on standard terms. It will be ready six years from launch, 2036 for a 2030 selection, with time on wing proven before entry into service. We will not speak for any airframer's plans or dates; that is theirs to announce."

(3) A P&W selection on the public record: `launch_if_selected` fires anyway, and `launch` then equals it.
