cfo.memo:
Low end first. Every plan's worst column is the same: Airbus launches NGSA without us, -27.76 in S3 and S6. Do Nothing adds that loss in S2 and S5 too, and gives up $14.0B at my weights.

My weights: S1 0.30, S2 0.20, S3 0.20, S4 0.05, S5 0.05, S6 0.10, S7 0.10. Nothing is launched and nothing is selected, so 0.40 sits where no airframe moves. My first read of any launch date is timing.

`launch_if_selected` is never below hold: +$13.69B weighted. Nothing is spent until a selection is on the record, then about $0.33B a year, 5.6% of a $6B envelope. The dividend is covered, debt stays on its pre-ASR path and no stretch is needed; it competes with buybacks only.

The unconditional `launch` loses 2.00 in S1 and S7 to gain 3.79 in S3 and S6. Edge +$0.34B; break-even odds 0.35, mine 0.43. It clears my ground 2, not the Board's +$0.5B; even a 2035 cancel reaches only +$0.47B. I would rather trade predictability for the opportunity for a lot of upside. We give up $0.34B for that, inside the cap.

One correction: if `launch` is ever chosen, the 2035 cancel cannot read "no selection". In S3 and S6 that kills the hedge where it pays off. Cancel where no new narrowbody is live, unless the 2035 hold row beats cancel.

The +3.79 is board mechanics: weight it, announce none of it. Booked: zero.

Joint Venture: Rolls-Royce is not on the record. Veto, ground 4. We'll cross that bridge when we get to it.

ops.proposal:
PROPOSAL (Eddy, operating seat; Calio decides).
- gtf2_solo: launch_if_selected. Launch 2030, ready 2036, no earlier than launch + 6. It fires only if a live airframe that is not yet in service selects a code with P&W in it (2, 6 or 7) this round, and only if GTF2 would be ready by that airframe's EIS. Otherwise we spend nothing. It ties the spend to a customer and keeps engineering on the fleet until a customer shows up [PX-0123][PX-0128]. Grid row 'GTF2 Solo if selected' minus 'GTF2: hold', S1-S7: 0 / +50.49 / 0 / +22.16 / +49.76 / 0 / 0. It is never below Do Nothing. S2, S4 and S5 are shared codes (6 and 7), so shared-source doctrine relief has to be declared.
- jv_with_rr: hold. Rolls-Royce has no commitment on the public record, and no live airframe carries code 1, 4, 5 or 7, so my technical conditions for a commit are not met. The gear and core stay ours [P-1233].
- Option B (unconditional launch) passes both my technical grounds, but I don't propose it. Under my rule I propose an unconditional launch only into a P&W code on the public record. An undisclosed hedge is Calio's call and has to clear Mitchill's gate; the edge 3.79 x (pS3+pS6) - 2.00 x (pS1+pS7) is his number, not mine.

ANSWERS TO CALIO'S ASKS.
1. Orders: as above.
2. Readiness: a 2030 launch is ready in 2036. NGSA 2037: 1 year of margin. fps 7-year 2037: 1 year. fps 10-year or via Embraer 2040: 4 years. A 2035 trigger is ready in 2041, too late for every 2030 airframe (2037 and 2040); confirmed. Proving durability before EIS: life-limited part (LLP) life, yes. All LLPs at full life at EIS is a design and certification commitment. I made it for the Advantage [PX-0128], and the Advantage was certified in 2025 with full-life LLPs [P-0785]. Time on wing can be validated before EIS only in severe-environment endurance testing, as we did on the Advantage [PX-0128]. Field time on wing takes fleet hours (company prior: about 1M hours to surface issues, profile.md section 3; inference). The basis is thin. It is one event, and my own date slipped: certification was aimed at mid-2024 and came in 2025. The company prior for a derivative's EIS is +1.5 to 2 years (profile.md section 3, inference). One year of margin is exactly what I want, and a slip like the Advantage's would use it up. My condition: the durability programme stays intact, and if anything gives, the date moves, not the testing. On this board the ready year is fixed at launch + 6, so the veto test passes.
3. Joint Venture readiness: if RR commits in 2030 and we commit in 2035, the Joint Venture forms in 2035 and its engine is ready in 2041. That serves no 2030 airframe (2037, 2040), only a 2035 launch (NGSA or fps 7-year EIS 2042; fps 10-year or Embraer 2045). With a 2030 GTF2 folded in, it is ready in 2036 and can serve the 2037 and 2040 EISs. Either way, the gear and core are not handed over.
4. Pacing parts: the 2030 bulletin and brief show no live P&W fleet, quality or supply problem, and the board does not model parts. I can't give a 2030 AOG count: my evidence stops at 10% AOG in June 2023 [PX-0120] and the roughly 350 AOG projected through 2026 [PX-0300]. Judgement (inference): from 2030 to about 2034 a GTF2 draws engineering and test-engine hardware, a handful of engine sets of castings, forgings and powder-metal disks. The real draw comes with the production ramp around 2035-36, and the company's last escape came from a ramp [P-1040]. Condition: GTF2 test hardware and the ramp take no pacing parts from the fleet's AOG recovery or from Hot Section kit insertion. The fleet comes first, reviewed weekly [PX-0123][PX-0131].
5. Engineering: yes, as one new development (inference). It is staffed from the Advantage engineering pool, which is shifting to other priorities [PX-0351, Mitchill's words, not mine]. The fleet's durability team (kit insertion, hot-and-harsh field issues) is ring-fenced. With jv_with_rr on hold there is no second programme, and a live GTF2 would fold into a formed Joint Venture as one programme.
6. Veto status: launch_if_selected passes on durability (2036 against 2037/2040) and on parts (no live problem shown). Unconditional launch: the same, it passes both. hold: not a Board item. jv_with_rr commit: neither of my grounds applies, so no veto, but my technical conditions are unmet, so I propose hold (the Board vetoes commit anyway). No binding veto invoked.

Public statement: no EIS earlier than 2036 and no airframer dates. Promise full-life LLPs at EIS and severe-environment validation, not field time on wing (advice, not binding).

vetoes.ground: Ground 1, durability not proven before entry into service. A standing condition, NOT invoked: the orders before me do not compress testing. If it ever arises, I would invoke it and it would bind under the team rule.

vetoes.plan: Public statement wording 'time on wing proven before entry into service'
vetoes.ground: Advice, not a veto: promise full-life LLPs at EIS and severe-environment validation, not field time on wing. No EIS earlier than 2036.

ops.would_change_mind_if: If an airframer puts a P&W code (2, 6 or 7) on the public record, I would propose an unconditional launch into it in its year. If a bulletin shows a live P&W fleet, quality or supply problem (an escape, rising AOG, pacing parts short), I would contain first and fail any unconditional launch on ground 2. If severe-environment test data or a reported slip takes GTF2 readiness past the EIS it serves (for a 2037 NGSA, anything later than 2037), I would invoke ground 1. If Rolls-Royce commits publicly or an airframe carries code 1, 4, 5 or 7, I would move the Joint Venture from hold to a technical-conditions review (ready by EIS; gear and core kept). If a 2030-triggered GTF2 loses its selection by 2035, I would flag the cancel test to Calio and Mitchill and propose hold as the default, since I have no evidence on cancelling.
ops.memo:
The bad number first: I can't give you a 2030 AOG count. My evidence stops at 10% of the fleet grounded in June 2023 and about 350 AOG projected through 2026. The bulletin shows no live fleet, quality or supply problem, and the board doesn't model parts, so the parts test passes on the board, not on data.

My proposal: gtf2_solo launch_if_selected, jv_with_rr hold. It ties the spend to a customer and keeps engineering on the fleet until one shows up.

Readiness: launch 2030, ready 2036. NGSA 2037 and fps 7-year 2037 give one year; fps 10-year or Embraer 2040 gives four. A 2035 trigger is ready 2041, too late for every 2030 airframe. Both my grounds pass on A and on B. B is Chris's call and Neil's gate, not my proposal: I propose launches into a P&W code on the record.

One year is the margin I want, and it's thin. The Advantage aimed at mid-2024 and certified in 2025; that's my own date slipping. So the durability programme stays intact: severe-environment testing, all life-limited parts at full life right at entry into service. If anything gives, the date moves, not the testing. Publicly, promise full-life parts and validated durability, not field time on wing. I said "not a surprise" once, five weeks before the recall.

decision.public_statement:
Bad news first. For too long the GTF fleet was not where it needed to be, and we own that. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF, and the fleet comes first. We keep inserting the Hot Section durability kit across the fleet, and no new programme takes parts or engineers away from that work. We control what we can control.

Pratt & Whitney will commit its next-generation geared turbofan, GTF2, in any round an airframer selects it, sole source or shared, on standard commercial terms. GTF2 will be ready six years from launch: 2036 for a 2030 commitment, and no earlier. Every life-limited part will be at full life at entry into service, and durability will be validated in severe-environment testing before then. If anything has to give, the date moves, not the testing.

We are making no Joint Venture commitment this round. We will not speak for any airframer's plans, dates or rates; those are theirs to announce. These are responsible bets with responsible paybacks.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: `gtf2_solo: launch_if_selected`, `jv_with_rr: hold`. Eddy proposed it, Mitchill recommends it, and the Board approves it at any weights. Overrides: none.

1. CONSTRAINT FIRST: safety and durability [PX-0035][PX-0073]
- Eddy's readiness check binds me, and it passes. GTF2 launched in 2030 is ready in 2036:
  - NGSA EIS 2037: 1 year of margin;
  - fps 7-year EIS 2037: 1 year;
  - fps 10-year or via Embraer EIS 2040: 4 years.
- A 2035 trigger would be ready in 2041, too late for any 2030 airframe. Only a 2030 order can answer a 2030 selection.
- One year of margin is thin. Eddy's own certification slipped from mid-2024 to 2025, and my operating dates have slipped by between one quarter and two years [PX-0017][PX-0098][PX-0104]. So I discount my own dates and take his condition: the durability programme stays intact, and if anything gives, the date moves, not the testing.
- Parts: the bulletin shows no live fleet, quality or supply problem. As Eddy says, this passes on the board, not on data. GTF2 test hardware and the ramp are ring-fenced away from the AOG recovery and kit insertion. The fleet beats a new engine [PX-0080].

2. BINDING VETOES, all respected
- Mitchill, ground 4, binding: no `jv_with_rr: commit`. Rolls-Royce is not on the record and no live airframe carries an RR code. I hold the Joint Venture.
- Mitchill's conditional ground-2 veto on `launch` is not invoked at his weights (+$0.34B edge with the corrected cancel). It does not bite, because I do not submit `launch`.
- Eddy: no binding veto. Both his grounds pass for `launch_if_selected`.
- The `overrides` field is empty.

3. THE GRID, rows S1-S7 ($B)
- `launch_if_selected`: 0 / +22.73 / -27.76 / +19.31 / +22.00 / -27.76 / 0.
- Do Nothing (`hold`): 0 / -27.76 / -27.76 / -2.85 / -27.76 / -27.76 / 0.
- Board item, `launch_if_selected` minus `hold`: 0 / +50.49 / 0 / +22.16 / +49.76 / 0 / 0. It is never negative.
- `launch` minus `launch_if_selected`: -2.00 / 0 / +3.79 / 0 / 0 / +3.79 / -2.00.

4. EXPECTED VALUES
- My weights: S1 0.28 / S2 0.22 / S3 0.17 / S4 0.05 / S5 0.08 / S6 0.10 / S7 0.10. I blended my frame prior toward Mitchill's timing read.

| Plan | My weights | Mitchill's weights |
|---|---:|---:|
| `launch_if_selected` + `hold` | +0.23 | -1.72 |
| `launch` + `hold` | +0.49 | -1.38 |
| Do Nothing | -15.97 | -15.41 |
| `launch_if_selected` + commit | +0.03 | |

- `launch_if_selected` against `hold`: +$16.20B at my weights, +$13.69B at Mitchill's.

5. THE HEDGE TEST
- Edge of `launch` over `launch_if_selected` = 3.79 × (pS3 + pS6) − 2.00 × (pS1 + pS7):

| Weights | Edge ($B) |
|---|---:|
| Mine | +0.26 |
| Mitchill's | +0.34 |
| My frame prior | +0.25 |
| Equal | +0.51 |

- At my weights and at Mitchill's, the edge is positive, so it clears Mitchill's ground 2. It is below the Board's +$0.5B franchise-defence bar, which only equal weights reach, just barely. Even crediting a 2035 cancel in S1 and S7, it reaches only +$0.39B (mine) and +$0.47B (Mitchill's). The Board wants the launch to stand without the option.
- Its case rests on S3 and S6 alone. S2, S4 and S5 are identical for both orders.
- The Board would veto `launch`, and I have no override against the Board. So `launch_if_selected` is both the doctrine order and the best plan that passes.

6. RESPONSIBLE BET: premium declared [PX-0010]
- Doctrine premium: $0.26B at my weights ($0.34B at Mitchill's). That is the PV I give up against the unconditional `launch` to keep the 'no new engine without a committed airframer' rule [P-0746][PX-0109][PX-0009].
- Objective premium: $0, explained in section 7.
- Total: $0.26B, inside the $1B cap.
- No Board item trails `hold`, so no Board premium is needed.

7. OBJECTIVE
- `launch_if_selected` and `launch` meet Restore credibility in the same columns: S2, S4 and S5 (p = 0.35).
- `launch_if_selected` meets Capitalise (ΔPV ≥ 0) in S1, S2, S4, S5 and S7 (p = 0.73). `launch` meets it only in S2, S4 and S5, because S1 and S7 come in at -2.00.
- So the objective does not favour `launch` on the grid. The off-grid chance of answering a 2035 NGSA switch to a P&W code is not booked (Mitchill's ground 4, confirmed).

8. MISS-A-CYCLE TEST [PX-0071][P-1347]
- Losing our half of the A320neo slot costs -27.76. `launch_if_selected` answers any 2030 selection in time.
- 'Miss a cycle' beats 'cross that bridge' only on visible demand. `launch_if_selected` makes the spend coincide with that demand.
- 'Miss a cycle' was said of RTX's businesses in general; applying it to GTF2 is inference.

9. SHARED-SOURCE DOCTRINE RELIEF, declared
- `launch_if_selected` fires on codes 6 and 7 as well as 2. Every selection column on this grid is shared: S2 (code 6), S4 (code 7), S5 (codes 7 and 6).
- I accept shared source against the sole-source rule [P-0746] as declared doctrine relief. The company accepts 40-50% of a shared platform [P-1292], and we aimed for about 40% of the A320neo [PX-0058].
- On NGSA it is also franchise defence (inference).

10. CANCEL TEST
- I adopt Mitchill's correction. For a triggered GTF2 that later loses its code: cancel in 2035 only if no live new narrowbody carries a P&W code, and only if the 2035 hold row does not beat the cancel row. The write-off is $1.67B and the cancel saves $0.33B.
- I reject the literal test 'cancel if no selection'.

11. DIVIDEND AND DEBT [PX-0081][P-0669][P-0686]
- Nothing is spent unless an airframer selects us. Then the cost is about $0.33B a year from 2030 to 2035, about 5.6% of the ~$6B envelope.
- On the analyst baseline, this competes with buybacks only. The dividend is covered, net debt is below 1x EBITDA by 2030E, and no envelope stretch is needed.

12. VALUE, NOT SHARE
- Standard terms. The Hot Section kit is charged. No concession in other moves or in the statement [PX-0055][PX-0100].

13. JOINT VENTURE
- `hold`. Revisit in 2035 on the trigger written into other moves.
- I have no record of my own here, so the view is doctrine plus Mitchill's and Eddy's tests.

14. BIASES, displayed
- Optimism on dates: I state no EIS, and I give no ready year before launch + 6.
- Incrementalism: I assumed the next single-aisle 'mid-next decade' [PX-0093]. Its failure mode, missing a round-1 selection, is closed by `launch_if_selected`.
- Supply-first caution: this is partly why I keep `launch_if_selected` over `launch`. Its cost is declared as the $0.26B premium.
- Architecture loyalty: GTF2 first, Joint Venture on hold. That is consistent with the unmet conditions, but flagged.

15. THIN RECORD
- I have made no launch decision, so my launch thresholds are inference (Medium).
- 'Miss a cycle' and 'demand visibility' are RTX-wide statements.
- My Joint Venture view is Low and rests on doctrine.

recommendations.text: The cancel test needs one wording fix. The private other move says 'cancel only if no live new narrowbody carries a P&W code'. Read literally, that would cancel a triggered GTF2 where NGSA or fps is live but has dropped P&W. That is the S3/S6-type path, where a ready GTF2 earns its +10 pp, and it is the error Mitchill corrected in my own guidance; the Board accepts his correction. Align the move with his memo: consider a cancel only where no new narrowbody is live at all, and keep GTF2 where an airframe is live without us. Any 2035 cancel will be a Board item, and it must beat hold on the 2035 grid. While a live airframe still carries a P&W code and GTF2 can meet its EIS, it must beat hold in every plausible column (Premature exit). The write-off is $1.67B, which saves only $0.33B.

Public statement, adopting Eddy's advice (a). 'Will commit GTF2 in any round an airframer selects it' should read 'where GTF2 can be ready by that airframe's entry into service'. A 2035 selection on a 2030 airframe could not be met (ready 2041 against an EIS of 2037 or 2040), and a promise we cannot keep costs the credibility the 2050 objective is meant to restore.

Back the absolute 'no new programme takes parts or engineers away' with the weekly pacing-parts review Eddy names, or soften it to a stated condition. Keep full-life LLPs at EIS and severe-environment validation written as a gate before EIS, not as a durability claim. The Board faces derivative claims over GTF oversight and wants no unproven durability promised.

Durability margin. One year between the 2036 ready year and a 2037 EIS is thin, and the Advantage's certification slipped about a year. If GTF2 is triggered, the 2035 package should report severe-environment test status and any slip against the EIS it serves. Eddy's parts pass rests on the board, not on data, so it should also give a GTF fleet AOG and pacing-parts count. The fleet beats a new engine.

Premium ledger. Report the Board-item premium (0 here) separately from Calio's doctrine premium of $0.26B against an unconditional launch, so that the company's $1B cap is tracked across rounds without double counting.

Next round, Miss a cycle. If no airframe launched in 2030, submit gtf2_solo: launch_if_selected again in 2035. Ready in 2041, it would meet a 2035 NGSA or fps 7-year (EIS 2042) and a 10-year or Embraer route (2045). An unconditional 2035 launch is ready in 2041 and can never be cancelled, so it must pass on the grid alone. It must also show an edge over launch_if_selected of at least +$0.5B on Mitchill's weights.

Joint Venture: hold until Rolls-Royce's commitment is on the public record or a live airframe carries code 1, 4, 5 or 7. Then re-test commit on the 2035 grid. A triggered GTF2 folds in and adds no new R&D. Any commitment shares risk and investment, never the gear or core technology.

Dividend and debt. If GTF2 fires, Mitchill's 2035 memo should confirm actual spend against the ~$6B envelope, the dividend covered and net debt still on its pre-ASR path. GTF2 competes with buybacks only.

rolls_royce.rationale:
DECISION (step 3, round 1, 2030). My proposal stands unchanged: `ultrafan_nb_solo: launch_if_selected`, with `jv_with_pw`, `ultrafan_wb` and `t1000_upgrade` at hold. Both memos recommend exactly these orders. McCabe co-signs. Watson invokes no Civil veto. Neither memo raises a binding veto against the package, and no company red line is breached, so nothing is struck and `overrides` stays empty.

1. GRID, WITH AND WITHOUT EACH BOARD ITEM (brief, S1-S9).
- Only one Board item: `launch_if_selected`. "UltraFan NB if selected" against "UltraFan NB: hold": 0 / +32.60 / 0 / +28.24 / +44.54 / 0 / 0 / 0 / 0. It is never below hold, so it passes the profit test under any weights.
- Worst column 0, unselected loss 0, against an $8B bill.
- Weights (mine, confirmed by McCabe): 0.30 / 0.10 / 0.15 / 0.10 / 0.05 / 0.10 / 0.10 / 0.05 / 0.05. Nothing is on the record, so each selection column gets 0.1, and S5 (both select us) gets 0.05.
- Expected gain: 0.1 x 32.60 + 0.1 x 28.24 + 0.05 x 44.54 = +8.31.
- Sensitivity (McCabe): at a per-airframer selection weight of 0.15 it is +12.47; at 0.05, +4.16; at 0.036, +2.99. It falls under the $3B cap only below about 0.036.

2. WHY CONDITIONAL, NOT UNCONDITIONAL.
- The unconditional "UltraFan NB Solo" is worth +5.20 expected, with a worst column of -8.00 (the full bill) in S1, S7, S8 and S9.
- Against the conditional form it gains +3.57 only in S3 and S6, at a combined weight of 0.25. It loses 8.00 in S1, S7, S8 and S9, at a combined weight of 0.50. Net: -3.11.
- It would win only if w(S3) + w(S6) > 2.24 x (w(S1) + w(S7) + w(S8) + w(S9)). Here that is 0.25 against 1.12.
- It also breaks the airframe-first red line [RX-0058, R-1005]. It is a Board veto, and McCabe withholds her co-signature.
- Timing: a 2035 launch is ready in 2042 and misses every airframe launched in 2030. This round's conditional order is the only route into one.

3. REJECTED ROWS (expected gain over hold; worst column).
- "if selected + commit to JV": +7.91; -4.00 in S7. A first commit with P&W not on the record: Board veto, red line, co-signature withheld.
- "hold + T1000 upgrade": -0.91; -0.98. Negative in every column. It counts only from the first Re-engine's entry into service, or 2042.
- "if selected + T1000 upgrade": +6.15; -5.98 against A in S2, S4 and S5. That is $5B of strain, more than the upgrade's own bill. Red line and Board veto.
- "hold + UltraFan WB": -3.69; -4.00. No Re-engine is on the record, and the shortfall is far above the Board's $1B cap for UltraFan WB.
- Our profile default of funding the Trent 1000 upgrade in round 1 is reversed on this board. I declare no premium for it and park it. Watson agrees: time on wing carries on in the fleet budget. That is doctrine applied to this grid, not my record.

4. PREMIUM: $0 on every item. The plan is the PV-best grid plan in expectation.
- Holding everything to stay inside Control's $4B line would be an objective premium of $8.31B ($4.16B at half weights). That is above the $3B cap, so I do not take it.

5. CONTROL'S METRICS FOR THE SUBMITTED PLAN, BY COLUMN (own NB money / strain / RR WB share 2050 / RR NB share 2050).
- S1: $0 / $0 / 58.0% / 0%
- S2: $8.0B / $0 / 58.0% / 36.7%
- S3: $0 / $0 / 58.0% / 0%
- S4: $8.0B / $0 / 58.0% / 40.5%
- S5: $8.0B / $0 / 58.0% / 51.2%
- S6 to S9: $0 / $0 / 58.0% / 0%
- Expected own NB exposure: 0.25 x $8B = $2.0B.
- STATED BREACH: in S2, S4 and S5 our own narrowbody money is $8.0B against the $4B bound. I accept it for three reasons: the trigger is a selection, the grid pays +28.24 to +44.54 there, and no other order reaches an airframe launched in 2030 (the Joint Venture is ready 2041 at the earliest on our side).
- McCabe confirms the breach cannot be cured. The earliest exit is 2035, when spend to date is already $5.7B.
- Strain is $0 in every column. WB share is 58%, above the 50% line, everywhere.

6. PATH TO A SHARED PROGRAMME, NEXT ROUND.
- If the order does not trigger and P&W commits on the record: I commit to the Joint Venture at our $4B share, inside the bound, with McCabe's co-signature on an expected gain above 0.
- If it triggers and P&W commits: a 2035 Joint Venture would fold the Solo in, with $5.71B spent to date, $1.71B written off and shares equalised with P&W. Control's metric would still read $5.7B. McCabe's prior is that the fold loses PV against keeping a selected Solo. I propose a fold only if that round's fold row beats keeping the Solo, and I will show the grid first.
- Once the order has triggered, any later widebody programme draws the $5B strain whatever its dates. Answering a Re-engine will therefore cost more, and I record that now.

7. FUNDING AND HURDLE (McCabe, co-signed).
- If triggered: $1.14B, about £0.84bn, a year for 2030-37, about £5.9bn in total. That is 22-23% of FY2026 free cash flow guidance and roughly the whole company-funded R&D line (£0.6-0.9bn a year, MS IS r129).
- It is new money above a flat envelope. I accept her advice on that, but it is not a sign-off ground.
- Funded from free cash flow. Buybacks give way first, and the dividend is untouched.
- No equity, no borrowing for distributions, leverage nowhere near 1.5x, net cash throughout.
- The triggered columns clear mid-to-high-teens hurdles: an implied IRR of about 30-45%. That is her inference.

8. MATURITY AND SUPPORT (Watson, no veto).
- A 2030 UltraFan NB is ready in 2037.
- Against an NGSA or fps 7-year launched in 2030 (entry into service 2037) the margin is zero. That is a named pass, not a veto. Test pacing is not compressed: if gearbox testing needs longer, the date moves, not the test plan.
- Against an fps 10-year or fps via Embraer (2040) the margin is 3 years.
- The trigger fires only if we are ready by entry into service, so the order passes by construction.
- Support plan carried in this package: partner MRO agreements on the Singapore model by 2034; the first partner shop and an EIS support team in place by 2036; high-performing suppliers only.
- The statement says "no earlier than seven years from launch" and "support in place before entry into service". It gives no airframer date.

9. RED-LINE CHECK ON FINAL ORDERS.
- No unconditional launch.
- No commit before P&W.
- No widebody programme beside a narrowbody order.
- No early date disclosed.
- No orphan programme: the conditional order spends nothing unless an airframe uses it.
- No equity.
- No item can lose more than its own bill in any column.
- All clear.

"I don't like options management": this is a choice with a trigger, not an option held open. It costs nothing until an airframer goes first.

recommendations.text: An airframe first. Carry narrowbody only as `ultrafan_nb_solo: launch_if_selected`. Show in the rationale why the conditional form beats an unconditional launch: the launch loses $8B in S1, S7, S8 and S9 for +3.57 in S3 and S6. A 7-year engine launched in 2035 would miss the 2037 entry into service of an airframe launched in 2030, so the conditional order this round is the only route into such an airframe.

Control's terms. Put the objective metrics for the submitted plan in the rationale. State plainly that a triggered Solo takes own narrowbody money to $8.0B (S2, S4, S5) against the $4B bound, and that the board accepts this only because the trigger is a selection. Set out now how the ExCo would move towards a shared programme next round. If P&W commits, a 2030 Solo would fold into the Joint Venture, but its spend to date still counts ($5.7B if folded in 2035). Show that grid before proposing it.

Keep widebody programmes off the record this round. The Trent 1000 upgrade is negative in every column: -0.98 in S1-S7 and -0.29 in S8-S9, because it counts only from the first Re-engine's entry into service, or 2042. Once it is on the record, it charges the $5B strain on any later narrowbody programme, the Joint Venture included, whatever the dates. That would close the narrowbody route Control's $4B bound points to. The widebody franchise test is not triggered: RR widebody share is 58% in every column and no Re-engine is on the record. Re-test the upgrade or UltraFan WB when a 787 or A350 Re-engine is on the record, or if 2040-2050 widebody share falls below 50%.

Public statement: few words, conditional and binding. Say that Rolls-Royce will launch UltraFan for any airframer that selects it, and that our preferred route is a partner, with the Joint Venture open to Pratt & Whitney. Give no entry into service earlier than launch plus seven years (2037 for a 2030 launch), and say nothing about an airframer's dates. A commitment by P&W on the record is our condition for committing next round.

Maturity and support. Watson should state the ready year against each airframe that might launch this round. UltraFan NB would be ready in 2037, which is zero margin against an NGSA or fps 7-year entry into service in 2037. A zero-margin pass is acceptable but should be named, with a support and MRO plan in place before entry into service and no compression of test pacing. The board will check his tests against the final orders.

Funding and balance sheet. McCabe should give capex a year if the Solo is triggered: about $1.14B, or £0.84bn, a year to 2037. Company-funded R&D is about £0.6-0.9bn a year in the 2026 analyst baseline (MS IS r129). She should confirm that no equity, no leverage above about 1.5x and no borrowing for distributions are needed, and say whether buybacks or other R&D give way first. We cut buybacks first, then the dividend, then new programme spend. The balance-sheet test is not applicable unless she invokes it.

frame.question: So, 2030. Nothing is on the record. The question is cash and quality of earnings, not share [RX-0054]. Do we put a narrowbody order on the table that costs nothing unless an airframer picks us: `ultrafan_nb_solo: launch_if_selected`, worth +28 to +45 $B if we are selected? The price is that a selection takes our own narrowbody money to $8B, against Control's $4B bound. Or do we hold everything, meet every Control line, and give up the only route into an airframe launched in 2030? Second question: does any widebody spend earn its keep this round? Frankly, the grid says no.

tests.numbers: If triggered, £0.84bn a year is roughly the whole company-funded R&D line (£0.6-0.9bn a year, MS IS r129); it cannot be redeployed inside a flat envelope, so investment rises above it in S2/S4/S5. Balance sheet before opportunity: it is funded from free cash flow with buybacks giving way, not from the balance sheet. Advice only, not a sign-off ground.

tests.name: Balance sheet
tests.threshold: No equity raise; no new borrowing to rebuild the balance sheet; leverage up to about 1-1.5x only for the right opportunity; never lever up for buybacks
tests.numbers: Board: debt $40B on EV $110B, unchanged by any order here. Real-world frame: net cash £2.1bn at 1H26 and £12.7-16.3bn in 2030E (GS/MS); a triggered £0.84bn a year (about £5.9bn cumulative) leaves net cash positive throughout. No equity, no borrowing for distributions, leverage nowhere near 1.5x. No balance-sheet veto applies.

tests.name: Joint Venture cost against Solo, and the fold
tests.threshold: Read the JV row against hold; spend beyond RR's $4B is written off on a fold and shares are equalised with P&W; already in the grid, not deducted again (inference)
tests.numbers: Not open this round: P&W not on record; on our side the JV forms no earlier than 2035, ready 2041, which misses a 2037 or 2040 EIS. Halves the bill ($4B against $8B). Fold arithmetic if A triggers and P&W commits: a JV formed in 2035 folds the Solo automatically; spend to date $8B x 5/7 = $5.71B, $1.71B written off, $2.29B of remaining bill avoided, RR's NB share cut from the Solo level (2050: 36.7% S2, 40.5% S4, 51.2% S5) to parity with P&W. Control's metric stays in breach at $5.7B. My brief holds no fold row this round; my prior (inference) is that the fold loses PV against keeping a selected Solo worth +28 to +45, so a round-2 commit with a live Solo is a fold decision, co-signed only if its row beats keeping the Solo.

tests.name: Cancel write-off
tests.threshold: Book the write-off arithmetic, not the sunk cost; cancel only a programme no live airframe flies
tests.numbers: Nothing to cancel this round. A triggered 2030 Solo cancelled in 2035: $8B x 5/7 = $5.71B write-off, and barred while the selecting airframe flies it. Control's $4B line could only be met by an exit within 3.5 years of launch; no round falls in that window, so a trigger fixes own NB money at no less than $5.7B.

tests.name: Short payback first
tests.threshold: State when each order starts to earn (inference)
tests.numbers: UltraFan NB (2030 trigger): ready 2037; earns from 2037 in S2 (NGSA EIS 2037) and from 2040 in S4 (fps 10-year EIS 2040). Joint Venture: forms 2035 at the earliest on our side, ready 2041. UltraFan WB: ready 2036; counts only from a Re-engine EIS (2035 if launched 2030, S8/S9). Trent 1000 upgrade: 3 years after launch and not before the first Re-engine EIS: 2035 in S8/S9, 2042 otherwise.

tests.name: Premium
tests.threshold: Price every doctrine or objective premium in $B; above $3B a round the PV-best order applies
tests.numbers: Recommended package = PV-best grid plan at base weights (+8.31; next best D +7.91, F +6.15, Solo + JV +5.60, C +5.20): premium $0 on every item. Holding everything to meet Control's $4B line would be an objective premium of $8.31B at base weights ($4.16B at half weights), above the $3B cap: the cap forces A unless the selection weight per airframer is below about 0.036.

tests.name: Control: own narrowbody money within $4B
tests.threshold: Own NB development money, committed or written off, <= $4B (Control's line; scored, never changes the payoff)
tests.numbers: Package A: $0.0B in S1/S3/S6/S7/S8/S9; $8.0B in S2/S4/S5 (breach, stated openly). Expected exposure 0.25 x $8B = $2.0B. Reason accepted: the trigger is a selection, the grid pays +28.24 to +44.54 there, and no other order reaches a 2030 airframe (a 2035 launch is ready 2042; a JV 2041). Not a veto ground: the CEO records the trade.

tests.name: Control: widebody never starved (NB + WB strain)
tests.threshold: Never hold an NB and a WB programme together; $5B strain whenever both are on record
tests.numbers: Package A: strain $0 in every column; RR WB share 2050 58.0% in every column (50% line not triggered); NB share 2050 36.7% / 40.5% / 51.2% in S2 / S4 / S5, 0% elsewhere. Airbus WB airframe share 25.2% in S8 noted; board engine share holds at 58%. Every WB programme stays off the record while A could trigger.

vetoes.plan: ultrafan_nb_solo: launch (unconditional)
vetoes.ground: Hurdle and unselected downside: no selection on the public record; -8.00 (full bill) in S1/S7/S8/S9, 0.50 of the weight; -3.11 expected against launch_if_selected; commits $8B in every column against Control's $4B. I withhold my co-signature.

vetoes.plan: jv_with_pw: commit
vetoes.ground: Hurdle: P&W's commitment is not on the public record and the row is -0.40 expected (-4.00 in S7, the full $4B share for no engine). I withhold my co-signature (joint sign-off on a commit is inference).

vetoes.plan: ultrafan_wb: launch (alone or beside launch_if_selected)
vetoes.ground: Hurdle and downside: -3.69 expected, worst -4.00 alone, above the $1B WB premium cap, no Re-engine on record; beside A -9.00 in S2/S4/S5, more than its own bill. I withhold my co-signature.

vetoes.plan: t1000_upgrade: launch beside ultrafan_nb_solo launch_if_selected (or launch, or a JV commit)
vetoes.ground: Downside: -5.98 against A in S2/S4/S5 (S7 against the JV row), more than its own $2B bill because the $5B strain stacks on it; -2.16 expected against A. Alone it is -0.91 and I would co-sign only with a CEO-declared premium; none is declared and I recommend hold.

vetoes.plan: Control's $4B narrowbody bound under launch_if_selected
vetoes.ground: Advice, not a veto: a trigger takes own NB money to $8.0B in S2/S4/S5 and cannot be cured below $5.7B by any later exit; priced and stated for the CEO's record. The flat-envelope overrun (about £0.84bn a year added) is likewise advice.

vetoes.plan: Balance-sheet vetoes (equity raise, leverage above about 1.5x, levering up for buybacks)
vetoes.ground: Not invoked: no order here needs equity or borrowing; net cash holds throughout even if A triggers.

cfo.would_change_mind_if: An airframer names UltraFan on the public record (P about 0.6): I would then test an unconditional launch against the +$2B bar (above 0 in 2035). P&W's Joint Venture commitment goes on the public record: I would co-sign a commit with expected gain above 0, but with a live Solo only if the round-2 fold row beats keeping the Solo. A 787 Re-engine naming UltraFan or an A350 Re-engine goes on the record: I would re-test UltraFan WB or the upgrade, but only with no narrowbody programme live. Selection weights fall below about 0.036 per airframer: A's expected gain drops under the $3B cap and holding for Control's line becomes a premium the CEO could declare. Delivered numbers move: RR widebody share heading below 50%, or a flying-hour shock that threatens cash breakeven, and I would re-phase spend. Watson's maturity veto on the zero-margin 2037 date binds whatever my numbers say.
cfo.memo:
Safety first, then the balance sheet. Nothing in this package touches either.

I confirm Tufan's weights: 0.30 / 0.10 / 0.15 / 0.10 / 0.05 / 0.10 / 0.10 / 0.05 / 0.05. On them, "UltraFan NB if selected" is worth +8.31 over hold; worst column 0; unselected loss 0. It is never below hold, so it passes under any weights. Halve the selection weights and it is +4.16; it drops under our $3B cap only below about 0.036 per airframer.

If it triggers: $8B over seven years, about $1.14B or £0.84bn a year, 22-23% of FY2026 free cash flow guidance and roughly the whole company-funded R&D line. That is new money, not a flat envelope. We fund it from free cash flow; buybacks give way first. No equity, no borrowing, net cash throughout. On a rough shape the triggered columns clear mid-to-high-teens hurdles comfortably; that is inference, and my record on launch economics is thin.

Control's bound: a trigger takes our own narrowbody money to $8.0B in S2, S4 and S5, against $4B, and it cannot be cured: by 2035, the earliest exit, spend to date is $5.7B. We accept that only because the trigger is a selection and nothing else reaches a 2030 airframe.

I co-sign launch_if_selected. I withhold on an unconditional launch (-8.00 in four columns), a Joint Venture commit (-0.40), UltraFan WB (-3.69) and the upgrade beside a narrowbody order (-5.98).

That's how you should hold it. That's our best view at the minute.

tests.name: Ready by EIS
tests.threshold: UltraFan NB ready at launch + 7 must be at or before the selecting airframe's EIS (launch + 7 <= EIS). A zero margin is a pass with a note: not a fail and not a veto ground. The Joint Venture engine is ready at formation + 6, or earlier with a folded Solo that is further along. A late engine is a fail as advice, not a veto.
tests.numbers: UltraFan NB if selected: launch 2030, ready 2037. NGSA launched 2030 (S2, S5 select us), EIS 2037: margin 0, PASS WITH NOTE. fps 7-year launched 2030, EIS 2037: margin 0, PASS WITH NOTE. fps 10-year or via Embraer launched 2030 (S4, S5, code 5), EIS 2040: margin 3 years, pass. The trigger fires only if a live airframe selects RR this round and the engine is ready by its EIS, so the order passes by construction. A 2035 UltraFan NB is ready 2042 and misses every 2030 airframe. Joint Venture: not in the orders; P&W is not committed; on our rule the earliest formation is 2035, ready 2041. That misses 2037 and 2040 EIS and would meet a 2035 NGSA or fps 7-year (EIS 2042) with 1 year of margin. Unconditional Solo: ready 2037 is not a maturity fail, but no airframe exists in S1/S7/S8/S9. Note on zero margin: the narrowbody gearbox sizing (a briefing constraint) is the maturity risk. If testing needs longer, the date moves and the test plan does not.

tests.name: No early date
tests.threshold: No statement or disclosure of an EIS or ready date earlier than launch + 7 for UltraFan NB (2037 for a 2030 launch), launch + 6 for UltraFan WB, or formation + 6 for the Joint Venture. Nothing on an airframer's dates.
tests.numbers: The CEO's draft says "Entry into service no earlier than seven years from launch", which is 2037 for a 2030 trigger and so equals launch + 7. It names no airframer date. The Joint Venture line carries no date. No other moves are drafted. Recommended addition: "support in place before entry into service". Do not say "ready for a 2037 airframe", which states an airframer's date and advertises zero margin. To be re-checked against the final statement and public other moves at step 4.

tests.name: Support before EIS
tests.threshold: RR has no narrowbody MRO scale (briefing constraint), so a support plan through partner shops must exist before any narrowbody EIS (inference). It must be carried in the package that holds a narrowbody trigger, launch or commit.
tests.numbers: Pass on the plan set out here, which must go into the CEO's rationale (otherwise it becomes ground (c) at step 4). On a trigger in 2030, with EIS no earlier than 2037: (1) Partner MRO agreements on the Singapore Joint Venture model signed by 2034. (2) The first partner shop inducting engines and an EIS support team in place by 2036: field service, a spares pool, repair technology, and the capacity to 'respond quickly and intervene' in the early years. That is 1 year before a 2037 EIS and 4 years before a 2040 fps 10-year EIS. (3) Narrowbody work placed with high-performing suppliers (GBP 685m of GBP 2.5bn external spend in 2023), none with underperformers. Gate dates are inference.

tests.name: Engineering load
tests.threshold: A narrowbody project (UltraFan NB or Joint Venture) beside a widebody project (UltraFan WB or Trent 1000 upgrade) costs a one-off $5B strain whatever the dates. Red lines: no UltraFan WB beside an UltraFan NB Solo unless both are selected; no upgrade while an UltraFan is in development or could be triggered.
tests.numbers: Plan A (UltraFan NB if selected, all else hold): no widebody programme, strain $0, 0 years of overlap in every column. Upgrade beside A: $5B strain in S2/S4/S5 (-5.98 against A); NB development 2030-37 against upgrade 2030-33 gives 3 years of overlap; red line. UltraFan WB beside A: $5B strain, development 2030-36 against 2030-37 gives 6 years of overlap; -9.00 against A in S2/S4/S5; red line. Joint Venture commit plus upgrade: -9.98 in S7. Forward note: once A triggers, any later widebody programme (for example UltraFan WB against a 2035 Re-engine) also draws the $5B, because the board charges it whatever the dates.

tests.name: Capacity and suppliers
tests.threshold: State RR engines a year for the plan from the brief's year table. The board has no capacity limit, so the result is not applicable unless the brief reports one. Flag a narrowbody ramp as needing partner MRO and high-performing supplier capacity (advice).
tests.numbers: Hold, or A untriggered: 0 NB plus 197 WB engines a year (58% of 340), 2026-2060. A triggered: NB share in 2050 of 36.7% / 40.5% / 51.2% (S2/S4/S5) of 4,000 NB engines gives 1,468 / 1,620 / 2,048 NB engines a year, or 1,665 / 1,817 / 2,245 in total. That is an 8-11x unit ramp on 197 today. For context, my own midterm ramp was widebody OE from 190 to 300-350 a year, with shop visits of 1,100-1,200 (I use my figure, not the 1,400-1,500 definition). MS has Trent deliveries rising from 259 (2025A) to 391 (2030E), with supply-chain charges ending only in 2028E. The narrowbody ramp lands after 2037, behind that widebody ramp. It needs partner MRO and high-performing suppliers. Advice, not a veto.

tests.name: Widebody dominance
tests.threshold: RR widebody engine share of at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050 on the brief's projection; time on wing is the lever (inference).
tests.numbers: 58% every year from 2026 to 2060 on hold (brief year table). Plan A is 58% in 2050 in all nine columns. The upgrade gives 63%, and UltraFan WB gives 68% in S8/S9 only. The test is not triggered. Exposure note: in S8 (787 Re-engine alone) Airbus's widebody airframe share falls from 41.2% to 25.2% in 2050. The board holds our engine share at 58%, but the real franchise is the sole-source A350, with the Trent XWB about 60% of the large fleet in 2027. Re-test UltraFan WB when a 787 or A350 Re-engine is on the record.

tests.name: Technology pull-through
tests.threshold: An idle or cancelled UltraFan still feeds the Trent fleet. A qualitative note; grid values are never adjusted for it.
tests.numbers: In S1, S3 and S6-S9, A does not trigger: no narrowbody spend, and UltraFan technology (25% better than the first Trent) keeps feeding time on wing on today's Trent fleet. Grid unchanged.

vetoes.plan: The CEO's lean: ultrafan_nb_solo launch_if_selected, with jv_with_pw, ultrafan_wb and t1000_upgrade at hold
vetoes.ground: NONE INVOKED. The engine is ready in 2037, against an EIS of 2037 (zero margin, a note) or 2040 (3 years). The draft statement has no early date. A partner-shop support plan is in place by 2036. No Civil ground applies.

vetoes.plan: RESERVED FOR STEP 4, NOT INVOKED NOW. It applies to any final statement or public other move that gives an UltraFan NB EIS or ready date before 2037 (launch + 7), counts on the engine before its ready year, or names an airframer's EIS as our date. It also applies to a final package whose trigger carries no partner-shop support plan before EIS.
vetoes.ground: Civil veto: an early disclosed date, or no support before EIS. It is not standing today. If it is triggered at the veto check, the team rule makes it binding and the CEO revises within it. The ground rests on attributed turns (RX-0296, RX-0284, RX-0283).

vetoes.plan: t1000_upgrade launch or ultrafan_wb launch beside the narrowbody order (or beside a Joint Venture commit)
vetoes.ground: Company red line, not a Civil veto ground. No upgrade while an UltraFan is in development or could be triggered, and no UltraFan WB beside an NB Solo unless both are selected. Each adds $5B of strain (-5.98 or -9.00 against A in S2/S4/S5). I would flag either as a red-line breach at step 4 for the CEO to strike.

vetoes.plan: ultrafan_nb_solo launch (unconditional)
vetoes.ground: Not a Civil ground: ready in 2037 is not compressed. Advice only: no airframe is on the record, it scores -8.00 in S1/S7/S8/S9, and it is the CEO's red line and a Board veto.

vetoes.plan: jv_with_pw commit this round
vetoes.ground: Not a Civil ground: the engine would be ready 6 years after formation. Advice: P&W's commitment is not on the record, and it scores -4.00 in S7 with no airframe to fly it. I lean to partnership, but the structure is the CEO's call. Hold.

vetoes.plan: Zero margin against an NGSA or fps 7-year EIS of 2037
vetoes.ground: A note, not a test fail and not a veto. The engine is ready exactly at EIS with no slack, and the narrowbody gearbox sizing is the maturity risk. Test pacing is not compressed to protect the date.

ops.would_change_mind_if: I would move to a binding veto if the final public statement or a public other move gives an UltraFan NB EIS or ready date before 2037, ties our date to an airframer's EIS, or counts on the engine in service before launch + 7. I would do the same if the partner-shop support plan (agreements by 2034, shop and EIS support team by 2036) is dropped from the package. If test maturity on the narrowbody gearbox showed a 7-year path cannot be met without compressing testing, I would tell the CEO the trigger should not be offered against a zero-margin 2037 EIS. In that case it would be offered only against a 2040 fps 10-year or via Embraer. If P&W's Joint Venture commitment goes on the public record (S7), I would back a commit next round: it halves our bill to $4B, P&W's gearbox answers the gearbox-sizing constraint, and the engine is ready 2041 if formed in 2035. If a 787 or A350 Re-engine goes on the record with no narrowbody programme held, or projected widebody share falls toward 50% in 2040-2050, widebody comes first and I would re-test UltraFan WB and the Trent 1000 upgrade. Named airline and airframer selections of UltraFan would strengthen the narrowbody case.
ops.memo:
Readiness, not hope. A 2030 UltraFan NB is ready in 2037. Against an NGSA or fps 7-year launched this round, that is zero margin; against an fps 10-year or via Embraer, three years. The trigger fires only if we are ready by EIS, so `launch_if_selected` passes. I accept zero margin on one condition: we pace the programme properly. Seven years of testing, narrowbody gearbox included. If maturity testing needs longer, the date moves, not the test plan.

Support comes first. We have no narrowbody MRO scale, so the plan is partner shops on our Singapore model: agreements by 2034, first shop inducting and an EIS support team in place by 2036, before a 2037 EIS, with work placed at high-performing suppliers. A triggered plan takes us from 197 engines a year to 1,665-2,245 by 2050.

Load: the conditional order alone carries no strain. Any widebody programme beside it is $5B and a red line. Once triggered, any later widebody programme also draws the $5B, so answering a Re-engine costs more. Widebody holds 58% in every column.

The Trent 1000 upgrade: I'm for durability, but this lever counts only from 2042 and blocks narrowbody. Park it; time on wing carries on in the fleet budget.

Statement: "no earlier than seven years from launch" is clean. Name no airframer dates; add "support in place before entry into service".

The $8B against Control's $4B is yours and Helen's to sign. No Civil veto. We're pacing that program properly.

other_moves.move: Narrowbody support plan before EIS (Watson)
other_moves.detail: Applies only if the conditional order triggers. Partner MRO agreements on our Singapore Joint Venture model signed by 2034. The first partner shop inducting engines and an EIS support team (field service, spares pool, repair technology) in place by 2036. That is ahead of an entry into service no earlier than 2037. Narrowbody work goes only to high-performing suppliers. The gate dates are internal and inference, and are not disclosed.

other_moves.move: Funding plan if triggered (McCabe)
other_moves.detail: $8B over 7 years, about $1.14B or £0.84bn a year for 2030-37, funded from free cash flow. Buybacks give way first. The 30-40% dividend payout is untouched. No equity, no borrowing for distributions, leverage nowhere near 1.5x, and net cash positive throughout.

other_moves.move: Open door to Pratt & Whitney on the Joint Venture
other_moves.detail: Our preferred route is a partner. We commit to the Joint Venture once P&W's commitment is on the public record. This round there is no commitment and no terms.

other_moves.move: Pricing discipline
other_moves.detail: No concessions to buy narrowbody or widebody share. Every new contract goes through the Investment Committee, and value is remunerated on a win-win basis [RX-0081, RX-0097].

decision.public_statement: So, plainly. Rolls-Royce will launch UltraFan for any airframer that selects it, in the round it selects it. Not before. Entry into service no earlier than seven years from launch, with support in place before entry into service. We don't need partnership for capability, but our preference is that: the Joint Venture is open to Pratt & Whitney, and we commit once its commitment is on the record. Widebody is our core, and we will not put it at risk. We won't do anything not profitable. We don't commit that easily; when we commit, we deliver.
decision.rationale:
DECISION (step 3, round 1, 2030). My proposal stands unchanged: `ultrafan_nb_solo: launch_if_selected`, with `jv_with_pw`, `ultrafan_wb` and `t1000_upgrade` at hold. Both memos recommend exactly these orders. McCabe co-signs. Watson invokes no Civil veto. Neither memo raises a binding veto against the package, and no company red line is breached, so nothing is struck and `overrides` stays empty.

1. GRID, WITH AND WITHOUT EACH BOARD ITEM (brief, S1-S9).
- Only one Board item: `launch_if_selected`. "UltraFan NB if selected" against "UltraFan NB: hold": 0 / +32.60 / 0 / +28.24 / +44.54 / 0 / 0 / 0 / 0. It is never below hold, so it passes the profit test under any weights.
- Worst column 0, unselected loss 0, against an $8B bill.
- Weights (mine, confirmed by McCabe): 0.30 / 0.10 / 0.15 / 0.10 / 0.05 / 0.10 / 0.10 / 0.05 / 0.05. Nothing is on the record, so each selection column gets 0.1, and S5 (both select us) gets 0.05.
- Expected gain: 0.1 x 32.60 + 0.1 x 28.24 + 0.05 x 44.54 = +8.31.
- Sensitivity (McCabe): at a per-airframer selection weight of 0.15 it is +12.47; at 0.05, +4.16; at 0.036, +2.99. It falls under the $3B cap only below about 0.036.

2. WHY CONDITIONAL, NOT UNCONDITIONAL.
- The unconditional "UltraFan NB Solo" is worth +5.20 expected, with a worst column of -8.00 (the full bill) in S1, S7, S8 and S9.
- Against the conditional form it gains +3.57 only in S3 and S6, at a combined weight of 0.25. It loses 8.00 in S1, S7, S8 and S9, at a combined weight of 0.50. Net: -3.11.
- It would win only if w(S3) + w(S6) > 2.24 x (w(S1) + w(S7) + w(S8) + w(S9)). Here that is 0.25 against 1.12.
- It also breaks the airframe-first red line [RX-0058, R-1005]. It is a Board veto, and McCabe withholds her co-signature.
- Timing: a 2035 launch is ready in 2042 and misses every airframe launched in 2030. This round's conditional order is the only route into one.

3. REJECTED ROWS (expected gain over hold; worst column).
- "if selected + commit to JV": +7.91; -4.00 in S7. A first commit with P&W not on the record: Board veto, red line, co-signature withheld.
- "hold + T1000 upgrade": -0.91; -0.98. Negative in every column. It counts only from the first Re-engine's entry into service, or 2042.
- "if selected + T1000 upgrade": +6.15; -5.98 against A in S2, S4 and S5. That is $5B of strain, more than the upgrade's own bill. Red line and Board veto.
- "hold + UltraFan WB": -3.69; -4.00. No Re-engine is on the record, and the shortfall is far above the Board's $1B cap for UltraFan WB.
- Our profile default of funding the Trent 1000 upgrade in round 1 is reversed on this board. I declare no premium for it and park it. Watson agrees: time on wing carries on in the fleet budget. That is doctrine applied to this grid, not my record.

4. PREMIUM: $0 on every item. The plan is the PV-best grid plan in expectation.
- Holding everything to stay inside Control's $4B line would be an objective premium of $8.31B ($4.16B at half weights). That is above the $3B cap, so I do not take it.

5. CONTROL'S METRICS FOR THE SUBMITTED PLAN, BY COLUMN (own NB money / strain / RR WB share 2050 / RR NB share 2050).
- S1: $0 / $0 / 58.0% / 0%
- S2: $8.0B / $0 / 58.0% / 36.7%
- S3: $0 / $0 / 58.0% / 0%
- S4: $8.0B / $0 / 58.0% / 40.5%
- S5: $8.0B / $0 / 58.0% / 51.2%
- S6 to S9: $0 / $0 / 58.0% / 0%
- Expected own NB exposure: 0.25 x $8B = $2.0B.
- STATED BREACH: in S2, S4 and S5 our own narrowbody money is $8.0B against the $4B bound. I accept it for three reasons: the trigger is a selection, the grid pays +28.24 to +44.54 there, and no other order reaches an airframe launched in 2030 (the Joint Venture is ready 2041 at the earliest on our side).
- McCabe confirms the breach cannot be cured. The earliest exit is 2035, when spend to date is already $5.7B.
- Strain is $0 in every column. WB share is 58%, above the 50% line, everywhere.

6. PATH TO A SHARED PROGRAMME, NEXT ROUND.
- If the order does not trigger and P&W commits on the record: I commit to the Joint Venture at our $4B share, inside the bound, with McCabe's co-signature on an expected gain above 0.
- If it triggers and P&W commits: a 2035 Joint Venture would fold the Solo in, with $5.71B spent to date, $1.71B written off and shares equalised with P&W. Control's metric would still read $5.7B. McCabe's prior is that the fold loses PV against keeping a selected Solo. I propose a fold only if that round's fold row beats keeping the Solo, and I will show the grid first.
- Once the order has triggered, any later widebody programme draws the $5B strain whatever its dates. Answering a Re-engine will therefore cost more, and I record that now.

7. FUNDING AND HURDLE (McCabe, co-signed).
- If triggered: $1.14B, about £0.84bn, a year for 2030-37, about £5.9bn in total. That is 22-23% of FY2026 free cash flow guidance and roughly the whole company-funded R&D line (£0.6-0.9bn a year, MS IS r129).
- It is new money above a flat envelope. I accept her advice on that, but it is not a sign-off ground.
- Funded from free cash flow. Buybacks give way first, and the dividend is untouched.
- No equity, no borrowing for distributions, leverage nowhere near 1.5x, net cash throughout.
- The triggered columns clear mid-to-high-teens hurdles: an implied IRR of about 30-45%. That is her inference.

8. MATURITY AND SUPPORT (Watson, no veto).
- A 2030 UltraFan NB is ready in 2037.
- Against an NGSA or fps 7-year launched in 2030 (entry into service 2037) the margin is zero. That is a named pass, not a veto. Test pacing is not compressed: if gearbox testing needs longer, the date moves, not the test plan.
- Against an fps 10-year or fps via Embraer (2040) the margin is 3 years.
- The trigger fires only if we are ready by entry into service, so the order passes by construction.

ops.note:
CONCUR. I invoke no Civil veto and find no red-line breach. I checked the final orders, the public statement, the public other move and the rationale.

1. MATURITY: PASS.
- `ultrafan_nb_solo: launch_if_selected` fires only if a live airframe selects us this round and we can be ready by its EIS.
- Launch 2030, ready 2037 (launch + 7).
- NGSA or fps 7-year launched in 2030: EIS 2037, so zero margin. That is a named pass and a note to the Board, not a fail and not a veto.
- fps 10-year or fps via Embraer: EIS 2040, so 3 years of margin.
- Testing is not compressed. If gearbox testing needs longer, the date moves, not the test plan.
- `jv_with_pw`, `ultrafan_wb` and `t1000_upgrade` are at hold, so there is nothing to test on them.

2. DATES DISCLOSED: PASS.
- The statement says "Entry into service no earlier than seven years from launch". For a 2030 launch that is 2037, equal to launch + 7 and never earlier.
- It also says "Not before" the selecting round. It names no airframer date and no calendar year.
- The public Joint Venture move ("commit once P&W's commitment is on the public record") gives no date. The Joint Venture engine is ready at formation + 6, so 2041 at the earliest for a 2035 formation.
- The rationale counts on no engine in service before its ready year.

3. SUPPORT BEFORE EIS: PASS.
- The partner-shop plan is in the package as a private other move: Singapore-model MRO agreements by 2034, and the first partner shop plus an EIS support team by 2036. That is one year ahead of the earliest EIS of 2037.
- Narrowbody work goes only to high-performing suppliers.
- The statement commits to "support in place before entry into service", which closes the step-4 ground I reserved.

4. LOAD AND RED LINES: CLEAR.
- No widebody programme is on record, so strain is $0 in every column.
- There is no UltraFan WB beside an NB Solo, no upgrade while an UltraFan is in development, no unconditional launch and no commit before P&W.

NOTES FOR THE BOARD (not vetoes):
(a) Zero margin against a 2037 EIS. Narrowbody gearbox sizing is the maturity risk.
(b) Capacity: if triggered, we go from 197 to 1,665-2,245 engines a year by 2050 (S2/S4/S5). That ramp needs partner MRO and high-performing suppliers.
(c) Control's $4B line: our own narrowbody money is $8.0B in S2/S4/S5. The CEO states this himself. It is his and Helen's to carry; it is not a Civil ground and not a company hard rule.
(d) Forward red line: once the order triggers, any UltraFan WB or Trent 1000 upgrade draws a one-off $5B strain. The upgrade stays barred while UltraFan NB is in development, to 2037.
(e) Wording advice for later rounds: "launch for any airframer that selects it" holds only where we can be ready by its EIS. A 2035 launch is ready in 2042, which misses 2030 airframes.

We're pacing that program properly.

recommendations.text: Maturity, our absolute priority. A 2037 EIS is zero margin. Watson should report the narrowbody gearbox test plan to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee each round. If maturity testing shows the 7-year path cannot be met without compressing testing, he should say so before any further trigger is offered against a 7-year airframe, and offer it only against a 2040 EIS. The date moves, never the test plan. The support gates (partner MRO agreements by 2034; a shop and an EIS support team by 2036) should be reported against their dates.

Control's terms and the shared route. If the order does not trigger and P&W's Joint Venture commitment is on the public record next round, bring `jv_with_pw: commit` at our $4B share. It needs McCabe's co-signature and a weighted value ≥ 0, and it brings us inside the bound. If the order triggers, own narrowbody money cannot fall below $5.7B. Propose no fold unless that round's fold row is shown against the row that keeps the Solo, column by column, and it pays. Never fold for Control's metric alone.

Widebody core. Keep UltraFan WB and the Trent 1000 upgrade off the record while UltraFan NB could be triggered or is in development. Once the order triggers, any widebody programme draws the one-off $5B strain whatever its dates, so responding to a Re-engine costs more. If a 787 or A350 Re-engine is on the record next round, or RR widebody share heads below 50% in 2040-2050, bring the rows for UltraFan WB and the upgrade beside the live narrowbody position. Show each item's worst column against its own bill and any declared premium against our caps ($3B in all, at most $1B for UltraFan WB). The A350 exposure in S8 (Airbus WB airframe share 25.2% in 2050) should be watched, though the board's engine share holds at 58%.

Funding discipline if triggered. About £0.84bn a year for 2030-37 is new money above a flat R&D envelope. McCabe should report each quarter how it is met from free cash flow and what it does to the buyback programme. Our order holds: buybacks give way first, then the dividend, then new programme spend. Any need for equity, leverage above about 1.5x or borrowing for distributions comes back to the board before it arises.

Public statement. The wording is clean on dates: no EIS earlier than seven years from launch, and no airframer dates. From next round, qualify "we will launch UltraFan for any airframer that selects it" with "where we can be ready by its entry into service" (Watson's note). A 2035 launch is ready in 2042 and cannot serve a 2030 airframe, and we should not promise what the maturity test forbids.

Airframe first, still. An unconditional `ultrafan_nb_solo: launch` comes to the board only once an airframer has named UltraFan on the public record, with McCabe's co-signature against the ExCo's bar (+$2B; above 0 in the 2035 round). Until then, narrowbody stays conditional. It is an option the company does not need.

board_review.note: The board approves. Product safety is and always must be our most important priority, and nothing here compresses it. The order launches only if an airframer selects us and we can be ready by its entry into service, 2037 at the earliest, with support in place first. It is never below hold in any column (+8.31 on McCabe's weights). Its worst case is 0 against an $8B bill, and no widebody programme sits beside it. McCabe co-signs; Watson raises no veto. We note openly that a selection takes our own narrowbody money to $8.0B against Control's $4B. We accept that trade only because it comes with an airframe and the grid pays for it. A partner remains our route to share the risk. And we do not want to underestimate the risks: zero margin against 2037 is the one to watch.
